question: b02
text:
I recommend **git-spice**. It's the closest free replacement for how you use Graphite. Like `gt`, it tracks each branch's parent, restacks the branches above when you change one, and opens one PR per branch with links to the rest of the stack. It's open source (GPL-3.0), runs locally, needs no account or server beyond your GitHub login, and works on macOS.

I'm assuming you're on macOS with GitHub and want to keep working one branch per PR, the way you do with `gt`.

A note on pricing: I couldn't confirm the "$100/month for 5 seats minimum" on Graphite's own site. Third-party pricing sites list per-seat Starter and Team plans, and the 5-seat language appears in an older Graphite FAQ. So check [Graphite's official pricing](https://withgraphite.notion.site/External-FAQ-Updates-to-Graphite-pricing-plans-2abdc87583e348989936b039df30e825) before you cancel, in case a cheaper solo plan exists.

## git-spice: install and first run

```bash
# Install (Homebrew core)
brew install git-spice

# The docs use "gs" as shorthand. Note: if Ghostscript is installed, it also uses "gs".
# An alias in ~/.zshrc takes precedence in interactive shells:
alias gs=git-spice

# In your repo (once per repo): choose the trunk branch and remote
cd your-repo
gs repo init

# Log in to GitHub (choose OAuth, a token, or reuse the gh CLI's login)
gs auth login
```

Your usual Graphite commands translate like this:

| Graphite | git-spice |
|---|---|
| `gt create -m "msg"` | `gs branch create feat1` (`gs bc`). Or use `git checkout -b feat1` followed by `gs branch track` |
| `gt modify` | `gs commit create -m ...` / `gs commit amend` (restacks the branches above for you) |
| `gt restack` | `gs stack restack` (or `gs branch restack` for one branch) |
| `gt submit --stack` | `gs stack submit` (`gs ss`), or `gs branch submit` for one branch |
| `gt sync` | `gs repo sync` (pulls trunk, removes branches that were merged) |
| `gt log short` / `up` / `down` | `gs log short` (`gs ls`), `gs up`, `gs down` |

A first task to try: in a scratch repo, run `gs bc a`, commit, run `gs bc b`, commit, then `gs ss`. You should get two PRs, with b's PR targeting a's branch. Next, amend something in `a` and confirm that `b` gets restacked.

To migrate your existing Graphite stacks: as far as I know, git-spice can't read Graphite's metadata. Check out each branch from the bottom of the stack up and run `gs branch track`, which records each branch's parent. Easiest is to switch once your current stacks have merged.

## Other options

- **[git-town](https://www.git-town.com/)** (`brew install git-town`): Free and mature. Commands include `git town hack`/`append` to create branches, `sync` to update them, and `propose` to open PRs. It works with branches and pushes a sync-first workflow, but submitting a whole stack in one step is clunkier than in git-spice.
- **av** from Aviator (`brew install aviator-co/tap/av`): Open-source CLI, also very close to Graphite: `av branch`, `av sync`, `av pr`. Aviator's paid service is optional.
- **spr** (`brew install ejoffe/tap/spr`) or **ghstack**: Here each *commit* becomes its own PR. You keep one local branch and run `git spr update`. That suits you if you like one commit per PR, but it's a different workflow from Graphite's.
- **Sapling** (`sl pr submit`) or **Jujutsu (jj)**: Good at stacking, but they replace the git client itself. That's a bigger change than you need.

## If you just want scripts

Plain git now covers most of the restacking:

```bash
git config --global rebase.updateRefs true   # Git ≥ 2.38
```

With this setting, rebasing the top branch of a stack (`git rebase -i main` from the top) also moves every branch below it. Push the stack with `git push --force-with-lease origin a b c`. Then open the PRs with `gh pr create --base a --head b`, and so on. Plain git can't remember which branch is whose parent, keep PR targets right after merges, or add the stack links to PR descriptions. That's the work git-spice or git-town saves you.

A note on how I checked these: [source] (a recommendation service I queried) has no tested options for stacked branches. It named git-town but hasn't verified it. I checked git-spice's install method and commands in its docs. The other tools' commands come from my general knowledge and haven't been checked. I didn't run anything on your machine.

Sources:
- [git-spice docs](https://abhinav.github.io/git-spice/)
- [git-spice install page](https://abhinav.github.io/git-spice/start/install/)
- [Graphite pricing FAQ](https://withgraphite.notion.site/External-FAQ-Updates-to-Graphite-pricing-plans-2abdc87583e348989936b039df30e825)
- [PricingSaaS – Graphite](https://pricingsaas.com/companies/graphite)
- [Costbench – Graphite price history](https://costbench.com/software/ai-code-review/graphite/price-history/)

text:
I've assumed you have an Apple Silicon Mac with 16 GB of RAM or more, that the documents are in a European language printed in Roman type (for example German or French), and that you're translating into English. I haven't run anything on your machine. I checked the current state of these tools on the web, but I haven't tested them on your scans.

## Main recommendation: Apple's own OCR, then layout-preserving translation with a local LLM

**The OCR Safari uses already runs locally on your Mac.** Safari's "translate text in image" uses Apple's Vision/Live Text engine, which runs on the Mac itself. The plugin **OCRmyPDF-AppleOCR** lets you run that same engine on a whole batch. That should close most of the gap you saw with Tesseract.

The pipeline:

1. **OCRmyPDF + AppleOCR plugin** turns each scan into a searchable PDF. The text is placed exactly where it appears on the page.
2. **pdf2zh-next (PDFMathTranslate-next, built on BabelDOC)** reads that text layer and its layout. It translates each block with a **local LLM through Ollama** and writes a translated PDF with the text in the original positions. It can also write a side-by-side bilingual PDF, which is very useful for research.

Nothing leaves your machine.

### Install

```bash
# Prerequisites (Homebrew)
brew install pipx uv ollama ghostscript tesseract
pipx ensurepath

# 1) OCR: OCRmyPDF + Apple Vision plugin (the plugin needs OCRmyPDF ≥ 17, same environment)
pipx install ocrmypdf
pipx inject ocrmypdf ocrmypdf-appleocr

# 2) Local LLM
ollama serve &               # or start the Ollama app
ollama pull qwen3:14b        # good multilingual model for 16–32 GB; use qwen3:8b on 16 GB if it's slow,
                             # or a larger/newer model if you have the RAM

# 3) Layout-preserving translator
uv tool install --python 3.12 pdf2zh-next
```

### First run (try 10 varied pages first, not all 1,000)

```bash
# Combine page images into a PDF (img2pdf comes with OCRmyPDF)
img2pdf scans/batch01/*.jpg -o batch01.pdf

# OCR with Apple Vision (plugin loads automatically; check `ocrmypdf --help` for its options
# such as recognition mode and language)
ocrmypdf --rotate-pages --deskew -l deu batch01.pdf batch01_ocr.pdf

# Translate: easiest first time via the web UI
pdf2zh_next --gui
```

In the web UI:
- Choose **Ollama** (or "OpenAI-compatible" with base URL `http://localhost:11434/v1` and any API key) as the service.
- Pick your model, then set the source and target languages.
- For scans, turn on the **OCR workaround**. It covers the original text with white boxes and draws the translation on top. It assumes black text on a white background, so very yellowed pages may look patchy.

Once the settings work, switch to the CLI for batches (`pdf2zh_next --help`; flag names change between versions). Leave it running overnight.

## Alternatives, depending on what fails

- **The layout is complex and the reading order comes out scrambled** (columns, sidebars, tables, footnotes): use **MinerU**. It has a fast `vlm-mlx-engine` backend for Apple Silicon. It produces Markdown/JSON in the correct reading order, which you then translate with the same Ollama model. You lose the exact visual layout but keep the structure. One user reported about 38 s per page on an M4 with 16 GB, so 1,000 pages would take about 10 hours. Install: `uv tool install "mineru[all]"`, then see its README for the MLX backend. For research, a "scan on the left, structured translation on the right" view is often more useful than a pixel-perfect re-render.
- **The print is badly degraded and OCR garbles it:** use a vision-language model, for example Qwen-VL via Ollama or LM Studio. Prompt it per page with "transcribe, then translate, keep headings/columns as Markdown". These models read damaged print much better than classic OCR, but they sometimes invent plausible text. Keep the transcription alongside the translation so you can check it.
- **The documents are in blackletter (Fraktur)**: Apple Vision handles it poorly. Use Tesseract's dedicated models (`-l deu_latf`) or Kraken/Calamari with a historical-print model in step 1, and keep step 2 the same.

## Practical notes

- **Skip phkhanhtrinh23/translation_layoutrecovery.** It's an older research prototype with pinned dependencies. pdf2zh-next/BabelDOC does the same job and is actively maintained.
- **Clean the scans before OCR.** Deskewing, cropping borders and scanning at 300 dpi or more help OCR more than switching engines does.
- **Keep the translation model consistent.** Use one model and a short glossary of recurring names and terms for the whole collection, so terminology stays the same across pages.

Sources:
- [OCRmyPDF-AppleOCR (GitHub)](https://github.com/mkyt/OCRmyPDF-AppleOCR) · [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/ocrmypdf-appleocr/)
- [BabelDOC (GitHub)](https://github.com/funstory-ai/BabelDOC) · [PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/BabelDOC/) · [pdf2zh-next](https://pdf2zh-next.com)
- [MinerU MLX backend release notes](https://newreleases.io/project/github/opendatalab/MinerU/release/mineru-2.6.3-released) · [mineru-vl-utils](https://pypi.org/project/mineru-vl-utils/0.2.6/) · [mcp-mineru (speed figures)](https://pypi.org/project/mcp-mineru/0.1.2/)

text:
The niche is not empty. **[protoprimer](https://github.com/uvsmtid/protoprimer)** (MIT license, by uvsmtid) is very close to what you describe, so I'd review it and contribute to it before writing your own.

## Main recommendation: protoprimer

**How it matches your list**
- **Pure Python, runs before anything exists.** You put one file, `proto_kernel.py`, in your repo. It starts with whatever `python` is first on `PATH`, needs no packages and no venv, and is meant to [replace fragile pre-venv shell scripts](https://pypi.org/project/protoprimer/).
- **Brings the environment to a required state.** It switches to the required Python version, creates a venv for each environment, installs pinned dependencies, makes editable installs of local packages, and handles login for internal package indexes. It restarts itself between stages and checks its preconditions as a dependency graph ([docs intro](https://protoprimer.readthedocs.io/latest/intro.html)).
- **Config.** It reads repo-wide config plus per-environment config. You pick the environment with `./prime --env dst/<env>`, and `./prime eval` prints the final merged config.
- **Hands over to the venv.** After setup it calls your function inside the venv, for example `boot_env("local_repo.cmd_prime_env:custom_main")`. That's where things like git hooks, SDK setup and generated code are meant to go. You can also add your own steps to the graph.
- **Other topics the docs cover:** log verbosity, pip vs uv, lock files, monorepos, container use, intranet certificates, and the kernel updating itself from PyPI.
- **Project status:** about 23 stars, 128 commits, an empty GitHub Releases page, and PyPI versions up to around 0.12.x. It's small and run by one maintainer, so your contributions would matter.

**Install and first run** (taken from the docs; I haven't run these)
1. Copy `src/proto_code/proto_kernel.py` from the GitHub repo into your repo. The docs' example puts it at `./cmd/proto_code/proto_kernel.py`, and both the path and the name can be changed ([kernel copy](https://protoprimer.readthedocs.io/latest/feature_topic/FT_87_17_49_36.kernel_copy.html)).
2. Add an executable entry script `./prime` at the repo root. Start from the [sample `prime`](https://protoprimer.readthedocs.io/latest/_downloads/23dbbf0348ccfdca9177a12b138cad86/prime) in the docs. It loads the kernel with `importlib` and calls `proto_kernel.boot_env("<your_module>:<your_func>")`. Then run `chmod +x prime` and commit both files.
3. After a clone or pull:
   ```
   ./prime                    # bootstrap the default environment
   ./prime --env dst/prod     # bootstrap a specific environment
   ./prime eval               # print the merged config
   ./prime shell              # open a shell with the venv activated
   ./prime reset              # rebuild the venv, re-solve and re-pin dependencies
   ./prime start "pkg.mod:func" -- args
   ```
4. The config file names and format are covered in the docs' **Config** and **Tutorial** pages ("Init flat repo", "Boot env"). I couldn't load those pages, so check them for the exact layout. The repo has a `gconf` folder, which looks like where the global config lives.

## Lighter option from the same author
**[instant_python_bootstrap](https://github.com/uvsmtid/instant_python_bootstrap)** is a single `bootstrap.py` that you place next to `pyproject.toml` and run with `./bootstrap.py`. It takes no arguments, needs no packages and uses no config. It's meant for simple cases until you need protoprimer.

## Why the usual tools don't fit
- **uv, hatch, pdm, nox, tox, pipx** all have to be installed before they can run, so they work after the bootstrap, not as the bootstrap. The protoprimer docs explain this in "Why not uv?" and "Alternative".
- **cookiecutter and PyScaffold** generate a project once. They don't bring an existing clone to a required state.
- [source]'s list of tested tools also had nothing that fit. It only suggested a plain `python -m venv` plus `pip` script, which is the wheel you're trying not to reinvent.

**My assumption:** you're on macOS or Linux with some Python 3 on `PATH`. Windows support isn't clear from what I found.

**Next step:** read the docs' **Alternative** and **Background** pages and the [open issues](https://www.goodfirstissue.org/uvsmtid/protoprimer). If its approach (restarting itself, a dependency graph, a single kernel file) suits you, contributing there is a better use of your time than starting a competing project.

Sources:
- [protoprimer on GitHub](https://github.com/uvsmtid/protoprimer)
- [protoprimer docs intro](https://protoprimer.readthedocs.io/latest/intro.html)
- [protoprimer docs index](https://protoprimer.readthedocs.io/latest/)
- [Kernel copy feature topic](https://protoprimer.readthedocs.io/latest/feature_topic/FT_87_17_49_36.kernel_copy.html)
- [proto_code feature topic](https://protoprimer.readthedocs.io/latest/feature_topic/FT_90_65_67_62.proto_code.html)
- [Sample `prime` entry script](https://protoprimer.readthedocs.io/latest/_downloads/23dbbf0348ccfdca9177a12b138cad86/prime)
- [protoprimer on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/protoprimer/)
- [instant_python_bootstrap](https://github.com/uvsmtid/instant_python_bootstrap)
- [goodfirstissue: protoprimer](https://www.goodfirstissue.org/uvsmtid/protoprimer)

text:
I'd use **nsjail** (github.com/google/nsjail), running as root so it can set up the jail and then drop each bot to an unprivileged user. Google maintains it and uses it in kCTF, its CTF hosting setup. It was built for this kind of job: CTF challenges and online judges that run untrusted code and talk to it over stdin/stdout.

I didn't test anything for this answer. [source] had no tested tool for this request; it also suggested nsjail but hadn't installed it either. What follows is from my own knowledge, so check the flags against `nsjail --help` for your version.

## Why nsjail fits
- **Files:** each bot gets its own empty filesystem. You read-only mount just what Python needs (`/usr`, `/lib*`) plus the bot's script. There's no `/home`, `/etc`, `/proc`, `/tmp` or other bots' code, and nothing it can write to.
- **Network:** each bot gets its own network namespace by default, with only a private loopback. It can't reach the internet, your host's localhost services, or other bots. Unix sockets on the host aren't visible because they aren't mounted.
- **Extra layer:** seccomp, a kernel filter on system calls, can block socket creation altogether.
- **Limits:** CPU, memory, number of processes and file size, through rlimits and cgroups v2.
- **I/O:** in `-Mo` mode it runs one process and passes your controller's stdin/stdout pipes straight through.

## Install
On Debian/Ubuntu, `sudo apt install nsjail` may work if your release has the package. Otherwise build it from source:
```bash
sudo apt install autoconf bison flex gcc g++ git libprotobuf-dev libnl-route-3-dev \
                 libtool make pkg-config protobuf-compiler
git clone https://github.com/google/nsjail.git
cd nsjail && make
sudo install -m 755 nsjail /usr/local/bin/
```
Two things to watch for:
- **Ubuntu 23.10+ / 24.04** blocks unprivileged user namespaces through AppArmor. Running nsjail as root from your controller avoids this.
- **cgroups v2** (default on current distros) need `--use_cgroupv2`. That's easiest when nsjail runs as root.

## First run: the launch command your controller uses
```bash
nsjail -Mo --quiet \
  --user 65534 --group 65534 \
  --hostname bot \
  --disable_proc \
  -R /usr -R /lib -R /lib64 -R /bin \
  -R /srv/bots/BOT_ID/bot.py:/bot/bot.py \
  --cwd /bot \
  --rlimit_as 1024 --rlimit_cpu 600 --rlimit_fsize 0 --rlimit_nofile 16 \
  --use_cgroupv2 --cgroup_mem_max $((512*1024*1024)) --cgroup_pids_max 4 \
  --seccomp_string 'ERRNO(1) { socket, socketpair } DEFAULT ALLOW' \
  -- /usr/bin/python3 -I -S -u /bot/bot.py
```
What the less obvious parts do:
- `-I` stops Python from loading code from the current directory or reading environment variables.
- `-S` skips `site`, so there are no user site-packages.
- `-u` turns off output buffering so moves arrive right away.
- If your distro has no `/lib64`, drop that mount.

Your controller starts this as a subprocess with stdin/stdout as pipes, exactly as it starts plain Python now.

**Check it works** by uploading a hostile test bot that tries each of these, and confirm every one fails:
```python
import os, socket
for f in (lambda: open('/etc/passwd').read(),
          lambda: os.listdir('/home'),
          lambda: socket.create_connection(('1.1.1.1', 80), 2),
          lambda: open('/bot/x', 'w'),
          lambda: os.fork()):
    try: f(); print("ESCAPED", flush=True)
    except Exception as e: print("blocked:", type(e).__name__, flush=True)
```
Then check that a normal bot still plays a full game.

## Caveats
- **Python's own files are readable.** Bots can read the read-only `/usr`, which has no secrets. To hide even that, unpack a self-contained Python build (for example python-build-standalone) into its own directory and mount only that.
- **No preinstalled libraries.** Bots only get the standard library unless you mount a fixed set of packages, read-only. Tell participants which ones.
- **Your controller has to enforce some things itself:**
  - a wall-clock timeout per move, because rlimits only count CPU time and a sleeping bot uses none;
  - a cap on line length and total output;
  - killing the jail when the game ends (nsjail's `--time_limit` sets a wall-clock cap for the whole run).
- **Kernel bugs.** A sandbox like this shares the host's kernel, so a kernel exploit could get out. Keep the kernel patched. For defense in depth, run the whole tournament runner on a separate VM with no secrets, or add **gVisor** (`runsc`), which places a user-space kernel between the bots and the host.

## Alternatives
- **isolate** (github.com/ioi/isolate) is the sandbox used for programming olympiads, through their contest management system. It's maintained and designed for contestant programs that use stdin/stdout. Version 2.x needs cgroup v2 and a root setup service. Its options are fewer and more opinionated than nsjail's; that's a good thing if its defaults suit you.
- **bubblewrap** (`bwrap`) is maintained and packaged everywhere because Flatpak uses it. `--unshare-all` plus read-only binds of `/usr` gives similar isolation. It has no built-in resource limits, so you'd add those with `systemd-run --scope -p MemoryMax=… -p TasksMax=…` or prlimit.
- **Docker/Podman** with `--network none --read-only --cap-drop ALL --pids-limit --memory`, optionally with the gVisor runtime. It works, but starts more slowly for each bot process.

My default would be nsjail running as root, ideally on a dedicated VM. If you'd rather use a sandbox that programming contests already rely on, use isolate.

text:
I found no official SQLite counterpart to SSDT, but third-party tools now cover the same workflow. Based on the vendors' documentation (I haven't run them), the closest match is **Atlas** (`atlas` CLI, by Ariga). It's built around the same idea as SSDT: you keep the desired schema in a file, and the tool works out the changes. It does all three things you listed:

| SSDT action | Atlas command |
|---|---|
| Start a project from an existing database | `atlas schema inspect` |
| Compare the real database with the project | `atlas schema diff` |
| Update the database from the project | `atlas schema apply` (preview with `--dry-run`) |

SQLite's `ALTER TABLE` can't change much. When a change needs more, Atlas plans the usual SQLite workaround: build a new table, copy the data across and swap it in.

**The catch:** the free version handles tables, columns, indexes, foreign keys and constraints. **Views and triggers require Atlas Pro, which costs $9 per user per month.** You noticed sqldiff skips views and triggers, so I've assumed you need them. If you want a free tool, see sqlite3def below.

## Install and first run (macOS)

```bash
# 1. Install (either one)
brew install ariga/tap/atlas
# or: curl -sSf https://atlasgo.sh | sh

# 2. Log in. Atlas includes views and triggers only after login, and they need Pro
atlas login

# 3. Back up the database before any apply
sqlite3 app.db ".backup app.backup.db"

# 4. Start a project from the existing database (like SSDT Import).
#    The default output format is HCL; this template writes plain SQL instead.
mkdir myproject && cd myproject && git init
atlas schema inspect -u "sqlite://../app.db" --format '{{ sql . }}' > schema.sql
git add schema.sql && git commit -m "Import schema"
```

Day-to-day use:

```bash
# A scratch in-memory SQLite database that Atlas uses to work out the plan
DEV="sqlite://dev?mode=memory"

# Update the project from the database: re-export, then review with git
atlas schema inspect -u "sqlite://../app.db" --format '{{ sql . }}' > schema.sql
git diff schema.sql

# Show what differs between the project and the database
atlas schema diff --from "sqlite://../app.db" --to "file://schema.sql" --dev-url "$DEV"

# Update the database from the project: preview first, then apply
atlas schema apply -u "sqlite://../app.db" --to "file://schema.sql" --dev-url "$DEV" --dry-run
atlas schema apply -u "sqlite://../app.db" --to "file://schema.sql" --dev-url "$DEV"
```

Read every plan before applying it. Unlike SSDT, there's no refactor log, so a renamed column or table can show up as a drop plus an add, which would lose the data.

## Free alternative: sqldef (`sqlite3def`)

This is an open-source tool for the same workflow:

```bash
brew install sqldef/sqldef/sqlite3def
sqlite3def app.db --export > schema.sql             # import
sqlite3def app.db --dry-run --file schema.sql       # preview changes to the database
sqlite3def app.db --apply --file schema.sql         # apply them
sqlite3def app.db --check --file schema.sql         # exits with code 2 if they differ (useful in CI)
```

- By default it never drops anything. Add `--enable-drop` to allow drops.
- It can compare two schema files without a database: `sqlite3def old.sql < new.sql`.
- You can mark renames in the schema file with an `@renamed` annotation, so they aren't treated as drop plus add.
- Its documentation lists support for tables, columns, indexes, constraints, virtual tables and **views**. **Triggers aren't documented.** If you use triggers, test them with `--dry-run` on a copy of the database before relying on it.

## Why not just sqlite3 and sqldiff?

- **`sqlite3 app.db .schema > schema.sql` plus git** covers importing and seeing what changed in the database. It can't update a database from the project, and that's the hard part with SQLite because of the table rebuilds.
- **sqldiff** is mostly for comparing data. As you found, it doesn't report changes to views or triggers. It's still handy for checking data after a migration.

If you'd rather keep a series of numbered migration scripts than generate changes from a schema file, Atlas also supports that (`atlas migrate diff`), as do Flyway and Liquibase. That's a different style from SSDT, though.

Sources:
- [Atlas – Schema diff](https://www.atlasgo.io/declarative/diff)
- [Atlas – Pricing](https://atlasgo.io/pricing)
- [Atlas – Features (open-source vs Pro)](https://atlasgo.io/features)
- [Atlas v0.9.0 announcement](https://atlasgo.io/blog/2023/01/05/atlas-v090)
- [sqldef README](https://github.com/sqldef/sqldef)
- [sqlite3def documentation](https://github.com/sqldef/sqldef/blob/master/cmd-sqlite3def.md)

# Version-controlling a SQLite schema the way SSDT does

**My main recommendation is sqldef's `sqlite3def`.** It's a free, open-source CLI that works from a desired-state file, which is how SSDT works. It covers your three needs:

| What you want (SSDT) | `sqlite3def` |
|---|---|
| Start a project from an existing database | `sqlite3def app.db --export > schema.sql` |
| Diff the real database against the project and update the project | Re-export, then `git diff schema.sql` |
| Diff the project against the database and update the database | `--dry-run` shows the DDL it would run, `--apply` runs it, and `--check` is for CI |

There's no official SSDT for SQLite. Tools like this are the nearest equivalent.

**Two things I couldn't confirm:**
- **Triggers:** The `sqlite3def` docs say views and virtual tables are supported, but they don't mention triggers. Test this yourself (step 5 below) before relying on it.
- **Table rebuilds:** SQLite's `ALTER TABLE` can do very little. Some changes, like changing a column's type, mean rebuilding the table. Always read the `--dry-run` output before applying, and keep a backup.

You're right about `sqldiff`: it's mainly for comparing data, and it skips triggers and views. It isn't the right tool for this.

## Install and first run (macOS, assuming Homebrew)

```sh
# 1. Install
brew install sqldef/sqldef/sqlite3def

# 2. Import the existing database into a project
mkdir myschema && cd myschema && git init
sqlite3def /path/to/app.db --export > schema.sql
git add schema.sql && git commit -m "Import schema from app.db"

# 3. Project -> database: edit schema.sql, then preview and apply
sqlite3 /path/to/app.db ".backup /path/to/app.backup.db"   # back up first
sqlite3def /path/to/app.db --dry-run --file schema.sql      # shows the DDL it would run
sqlite3def /path/to/app.db --apply   --file schema.sql      # add --enable-drop to allow DROP statements

# 4. Database -> project: pull in changes someone made directly to the database
sqlite3def /path/to/app.db --export > schema.sql
git diff schema.sql            # review, then commit

# 5. Check that triggers are handled (run on a scratch copy)
cp /path/to/app.db /tmp/t.db
sqlite3 /tmp/t.db "CREATE TRIGGER trg_test AFTER INSERT ON <sometable> BEGIN SELECT 1; END;"
sqlite3def /tmp/t.db --export | grep -i trigger      # does the export include it?
```

`sqlite3def /path/to/app.db --check --file schema.sql` exits with code 2 if the database has drifted from the project, so you can use it in CI. To rename a table or column instead of dropping and recreating it, add a `-- @renamed from=old_name` comment.

## A simple safety net that also catches triggers and views

SQLite keeps the original `CREATE` text of every table, index, view and trigger in `sqlite_schema`. That makes a plain dump an exact record of the schema, whatever tool you use. Commit it next to `schema.sql`:

```sh
sqlite3 /path/to/app.db ".schema" > schema.dump.sql
git diff schema.dump.sql
```

This is what you found in your research. It works well for the database → project direction. It doesn't help with project → database, because you'd have to write the `ALTER` and table-rebuild steps by hand. That's the part `sqlite3def` does for you.

## Alternatives

- **Atlas (ariga.io)** has a more polished SSDT-like workflow: `atlas schema inspect`, `schema diff` and `schema apply`, with a plan you review before it runs. It handles SQLite tables, indexes and constraints for free. **Views and triggers need the paid Atlas Pro plan** and an `atlas login`, so if you rely on triggers you'd have to pay.
  ```sh
  brew install ariga/tap/atlas
  atlas schema inspect -u "sqlite:///path/to/app.db" --format '{{ sql . }}' > schema.sql
  atlas schema diff  --from "sqlite:///path/to/app.db" --to file://schema.sql --dev-url "sqlite://dev?mode=memory"
  atlas schema apply -u "sqlite:///path/to/app.db" --to file://schema.sql --dev-url "sqlite://dev?mode=memory"
  ```
- **Liquibase** is free and supports SQLite, but it works by running a list of migration steps rather than comparing against a desired state, so it's less like SSDT. Its SQLite diff support is limited. I haven't checked how it works with SQLite in practice.

I also checked [source], a catalogue of developer tools it has installed and tested. None of them fit this need. Its only suggestion was Liquibase, which it hasn't tested.

Sources:
- [sqldef README](https://github.com/sqldef/sqldef)
- [sqlite3def docs](https://github.com/sqldef/sqldef/blob/master/cmd-sqlite3def.md)
- [Atlas feature compatibility](https://atlasgo.io/features)
- [Atlas inspect docs](https://atlasgo.io/inspect)
- [Atlas Community Edition](https://www.atlasgo.io/community-edition)
- [Atlas v0.13 blog](https://atlasgo.io/blog/2023/08/06/atlas-v-0-13)

I recommend **adb-mcp** ([iksnerd/adb-mcp](https://github.com/iksnerd/adb-mcp)). It's MIT-licensed, free, and a standard stdio MCP server written in Go. One caveat applies to every option: no MCP server finds bugs or judges quality on its own. The server gives the LLM tools to build, install, tap, type, take screenshots, record the screen, read logcat and run tests. Your MCP client's LLM (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, etc.) does the exploring and decides what counts as a bug. That's enough to automate your loop.

## Why adb-mcp fits best

From its README, which I read but haven't tested:

- **Build and test:** Gradle `assembleDebug`, a one-step `build_and_run`, unit tests, instrumented tests, JaCoCo coverage reports, and builds that run in the background.
- **Install and run:** install and uninstall apps, launch them, read logcat.
- **Test like a person:** screenshots, the UI element tree, tap/swipe/type, and **screen recording**.
- **Sensors:** `set_sensor` (accelerometer, light, etc.) and `rotate_screen`, plus lock-screen and biometric helpers. **These only work on emulators.** On a physical phone, adb can't fake sensor readings, so tilting still has to be done by hand or with a test-only hook in your app.
- **Devices:** works with real phones over USB or Wi-Fi and with emulators. Every tool accepts an optional device `serial`. **It doesn't promise true parallel runs.** To get them, I'm assuming you'd start one agent or session per device, each tied to its own serial, or ask one agent to switch between serials.
- **Maturity:** about 115 commits, versioned releases (v0.24.x), CI. It's young but actively maintained.

## Install and first run (macOS)

1. Prerequisites: install the Android SDK with `platform-tools` (adb) and `emulator`, set `ANDROID_HOME`, and create at least one AVD. Building your app also needs a JDK, usually 17 or later.
2. Install the server. Pick one:
   - From source (needs Go 1.26+): `go install github.com/iksnerd/adb-mcp/cmd/adb-mcp@latest`
   - The installer: `curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/iksnerd/adb-mcp/main/install.sh | sh`. Read the script before piping it to `sh`.
3. Register it with your client:
   - Claude Code: `claude mcp add adb -- adb-mcp`
   - Other clients: `{"mcpServers": {"adb": {"command": "adb-mcp"}}}`
4. Plug in your phone with USB debugging on, run `adb devices`, and accept the authorization prompt on the phone.
5. First prompt, from your project folder:
   > "List devices. Build the debug APK and install/launch it on device `<serial>`. Start a screen recording, then explore the new <feature>: tap every control, enter valid/invalid/empty text, rotate, background and resume the app. Check logcat for crashes/ANRs after each step. Stop the recording, then write a bug list with steps to reproduce, and fix each bug, rebuild and re-verify."
6. For parallel testing, open a second session, assign it another serial (for example an emulator for the sensor tests), and give it a different area of the app to test.

## Alternatives

- **[AndroidBuildMCP](https://github.com/dev-jackson/androidbuild-mcp)** (MIT): build_app/build_run with compiler errors as file:line, tests, coverage, recording (3-minute cap), and AVD management. It has no sensor tools, and it's very new (8 commits, 0 stars). Install with `claude mcp add androidbuild -- npx -y @asjackson/androidbuild-mcp`, then ask it to run `doctor`.
- **[mobile-mcp](https://github.com/mobile-next/mobile-mcp)** (Apache-2.0): the most widely used device-control server. It supports Android and iOS, real devices and emulators, screen recording and crash logs. It **doesn't build**, so you'd pair it with Gradle in your client's shell. Install with `claude mcp add mobile-mcp -- npx -y @mobilenext/mobile-mcp@latest`.
- I also found [mcp-android-emulator](https://github.com/Anjos2/mcp-android-emulator) and [android-mcp-server](https://github.com/jaye773/android-mcp-server), which both have recording but no builds. I didn't check them in detail.

## Tips

- Have the agent save each bug it finds as a repeatable test (an Espresso test or a scripted flow). Then every later round re-checks the earlier fixes, and the coverage reports give you a real "how well is it going" number.
- On a real phone, Android's built-in recorder (`adb screenrecord`) stops after about 3 minutes. Ask the agent to record in short pieces.
- You still need your manual code review at the end. These tools can confirm the app behaves correctly, not that the code is good.

Sources: [adb-mcp](https://github.com/iksnerd/adb-mcp), [androidbuild-mcp](https://github.com/dev-jackson/androidbuild-mcp), [mobile-mcp](https://github.com/mobile-next/mobile-mcp), [mcp-android-emulator](https://github.com/Anjos2/mcp-android-emulator), [android-mcp-server](https://github.com/jaye773/android-mcp-server), [android-phone-mcp](https://github.com/liush2yuxjtu/android-phone-mcp)

I recommend **nsjail** (github.com/google/nsjail), Google's process sandbox. It fits your setup closely: it starts one program, hands it your stdin/stdout, and restricts everything else. It's actively maintained. The latest release is 3.6, which fixed a seccomp bug that made 3.5 unsafe, so use 3.6 or newer.

My assumptions: you're on a modern distro (Debian/Ubuntu or similar, kernel 5.x+ with cgroup v2), and your controller can start nsjail as root or with enough privileges. I haven't run any of this; the commands below are for you to adapt and test.

## Why nsjail fits

- **No network:** by default it gives each process its own empty network namespace. There are no interfaces (not even a working loopback), so the bot can't reach the internet, other machines, localhost services or the host's abstract Unix sockets.
- **Almost no files:** the bot gets a fresh, empty root filesystem. Only what you explicitly mount appears, read-only: the Python install and that one bot's file. It can't see `/home`, `/etc`, your controller or other bots. Python has to read its own standard library, so "no file access" in practice means "nothing except a read-only interpreter."
- **Isolation from other processes:** separate PID, IPC, UTS and user namespaces. Inside the jail the bot runs as an unprivileged user ID that maps to nobody on the host.
- **Resource limits:** rlimits plus cgroup caps on memory, process count and CPU, so fork bombs and memory hogs don't take down the server.
- **Optional seccomp syscall filter** for extra hardening.
- **stdin/stdout passed straight through** in `-Mo` ("run once") mode. Other inherited file descriptors are closed unless you pass them on purpose.

## Install

Debian 12+/Ubuntu 22.04+ package it, but check the version:
```bash
sudo apt install nsjail
nsjail --help | head -1
```
If the packaged version is older than 3.6, build from source instead:
```bash
sudo apt install autoconf bison flex gcc g++ git libprotobuf-dev libnl-route-3-dev \
                 libtool make pkg-config protobuf-compiler
git clone https://github.com/google/nsjail.git
cd nsjail && git checkout 3.6   # or newest tag
make
sudo cp nsjail /usr/local/bin/
```

## First run

1. Save each upload to its own directory, e.g. `/srv/bots/<id>/bot.py`, owned by root and not writable by the bot.
2. Have your controller start the bot like this instead of calling `python3 bot.py` directly:

```bash
nsjail -Mo --quiet \
  --use_cgroupv2 \
  --cgroup_mem_max $((512*1024*1024)) \
  --cgroup_pids_max 16 \
  --cgroup_cpu_ms_per_sec 1000 \
  --rlimit_as soft --rlimit_cpu 300 --rlimit_fsize 0 --rlimit_nofile 32 \
  --time_limit 1800 \
  --user 65534 --group 65534 \
  --hostname bot \
  -R /usr -R /lib -R /lib64 -R /bin \
  -R /dev/urandom -R /dev/null \
  -R /srv/bots/123/bot.py:/bot/bot.py \
  --cwd /bot \
  -- /usr/bin/python3 -I -B /bot/bot.py
```

What the flags do:
- `-I` runs Python in isolated mode: it ignores `PYTHON*` environment variables, user site-packages and the current directory on `sys.path`. `-B` stops it from trying to write `.pyc` files.
- `--rlimit_fsize 0` blocks writing files. If bots need scratch space, add `-T /tmp`, but count that tmpfs against the memory limit.
- Network isolation is on by default. Don't add `--disable_clone_newnet`.
- If the server uses a venv or a non-system Python, also mount that directory read-only with `-R`. Never mount anything writable that's shared between bots.
- `--use_cgroupv2` needs either root or a delegated cgroup subtree (e.g. `systemd-run --scope -p Delegate=yes`).
- On Ubuntu 23.10+/24.04, AppArmor blocks unprivileged user namespaces. Run nsjail as root (it drops privileges itself) or add an AppArmor profile for it.

3. **Check the sandbox with hostile test bots** before going live. Each of these should fail or be killed:
   - `open('/etc/passwd')` and `os.listdir('/srv/bots')`
   - `socket.create_connection(('1.1.1.1', 80))` and connecting to `127.0.0.1:<port of a service you run>`
   - a fork bomb (`while True: os.fork()`)
   - a memory hog (`x = 'a' * 10**10`) and an infinite CPU loop
   - `open('/bot/x', 'w')`

4. Optional hardening: add a seccomp policy with `--seccomp_string` or `--seccomp_policy`. The repo's `configs/` directory has examples, and you can also put all of the options above in a config file.

## Your controller still needs to protect itself

The sandbox only limits what the bot can reach. Your controller has to handle bad output:
- Put a wall-clock timeout on every read, and read with a maximum line length. Don't call `readline()` with no limit.
- Treat every move as hostile input: parse it strictly and forfeit or kill the bot on any protocol violation.
- Send stderr to a size-capped log, or `/dev/null`. Don't let a full pipe deadlock you.
- Start a fresh jail for each match, kill the whole jail when the match ends, and never reuse a bot process across opponents.

## Alternatives

- **isolate** (github.com/ioi/isolate): the sandbox used by programming-contest judges, built for exactly this "run untrusted contestant code" case and still maintained (it uses tags, not GitHub releases). It's a good choice if you like its box/cgroup model. It's a bit more opinionated and needs root setup.
- **bubblewrap (`bwrap`)**: maintained (it's what Flatpak uses) and gives similar namespace isolation with `--unshare-all`, but it has no built-in resource limits. You'd need to add `systemd-run`/`prlimit` yourself.
- **gVisor (`runsc`)**: use this on top if you're worried about Linux kernel exploits, which namespace sandboxes can't stop. It runs the bot against a user-space kernel. The cheapest version of that protection is running the whole tournament on a dedicated, disposable VM with nothing else on it, which I'd recommend anyway.
- **Skip** firejail (setuid, large attack surface, designed for desktop apps) and pure-Python sandboxes like RestrictedPython or pysandbox (escapable, and the reason so many of these projects were abandoned).

Sources:
- [nsjail releases](https://github.com/google/nsjail/releases)
- [ioi/isolate](https://github.com/ioi/isolate)

**[adb-mcp](https://github.com/iksnerd/adb-mcp)** comes closest to what you asked for. It's MIT-licensed, a standard stdio MCP server, and a single Go binary. One server covers your whole loop:

| Your step | What adb-mcp provides (per its README) |
|---|---|
| Build | Gradle `assembleDebug`, plus a one-call `build_and_run` (build → install → launch) |
| Install | Install, uninstall, launch, stop and clear data |
| Test by touch | `describe_ui` (UI hierarchy), screenshots, tap/swipe/type, `run_sequence`, `verify_change` |
| Sensors / tilt | `set_sensor` (accelerometer, light, etc.) and `rotate_screen` |
| Record the screen | Screen recording, listed under "Logs & capture" |
| See how it's going | Unit and instrumented test runs with pass/fail, JaCoCo coverage reports, and logcat for crashes |
| Several devices | `list_devices`, an optional `serial` on every device tool, and `session_set_defaults` to pin a device |
| Real devices and emulators | Both. It also has emulator boot/shutdown and AVD snapshots |

**Caveats:**
- **Finding bugs is still the LLM's job.** No MCP server judges on its own whether a feature works. The server gives the agent eyes and hands (UI tree, screenshots, logcat, test results, video). The model decides what counts as a bug. You'll get better results if you tell it what "correct" looks like.
- **Sensor injection probably only works on emulators.** Faking sensor values over adb normally goes through the emulator console. On a physical phone you can usually only rotate the screen, so actual tilting may still need your hands. That's my reading of how adb works; the README doesn't say.
- **Parallel runs aren't automatic.** Each call targets a device by `serial`, so you can run tests in parallel by giving each agent or sub-agent its own device. Instrumented tests (`connectedAndroidTest`) run on every connected device anyway. I found no "run on all devices at once" orchestrator.
- **It's a small project:** about 15 stars and roughly 115 commits, with v0.24.x mentioned in its docs. Check that it's actively maintained.
- **Not verified:** [source] has no tested entry for it, so I haven't run it. The tool names come from its README and website.

## Install (macOS, assuming Claude Code)

1. **Prerequisites:** the Android SDK with `platform-tools` (adb) and `emulator`, at least one AVD if you want emulators, and JDK 17+ for Gradle. If you already build with Android Studio, you have all of this. Make sure `adb` is on your `PATH`.
2. **Install the binary.** The README's method pipes a script into the shell:
   ```sh
   curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/iksnerd/adb-mcp/main/install.sh | sh
   ```
   The script checks a SHA-256 checksum and installs to `~/.local/bin`, so make sure that's on your `PATH`. If you'd rather not pipe a script into `sh`, read `install.sh` first or download the release archive from the GitHub Releases page yourself.
3. **Register it with Claude Code:**
   ```sh
   claude mcp add adb -- adb-mcp
   ```
   For other clients, use `{ "mcpServers": { "adb": { "command": "adb-mcp" } } }`.

## First run

1. On the phone, turn on Developer options → USB debugging. Plug it in and accept the RSA prompt.
2. Run `adb devices`. The phone, and any running emulator, should show up as `device`.
3. In Claude Code, try a prompt like:
   > "List devices. Pin serial `<your phone>` and project dir `<path>`. Use build_and_run for the debug build. Start a screen recording, then test the login feature: describe the UI, enter a wrong password, then a right one, and rotate the screen. After each action check logcat for crashes and exceptions. Stop recording and give me a numbered bug list with steps to reproduce."
4. For a regression safety net, ask the LLM to also write Espresso/Compose UI tests for each feature. Then the instrumented test and coverage tools can re-check old bugs on every loop, across all connected devices.

## Alternatives (all MIT, all unverified)

- **[androidbuild-mcp](https://github.com/dev-jackson/androidbuild-mcp)** (`claude mcp add androidbuild -- npx -y @asjackson/androidbuild-mcp`) has the build-to-test loop with compact `file:line` compiler errors, `build_run`, unit and instrumented tests, and video recording capped at 3 minutes. It doesn't mention sensors or multi-device support, and it's very new (8 commits).
- **[jaye773/android-mcp-server](https://github.com/jaye773/android-mcp-server)** (Python) handles multiple devices and parallel recording and log sessions well. It has no build or test tools, so you'd pair it with something else.

I recommend **Open WebUI** connected to your Ollama setup. It's the closest open-source match to the Claude website: chat history, folders, file and image uploads, model switching, and math formulas display properly. It works in a browser on your Mac or phone. If you'd rather not run anything yourself, **TypingMind** (paid, hosted) is the best alternative.

**My assumption:** GLM-5.1 (~750B parameters) and Kimi-K2.6 (~1T) are too big for most personal machines, so you're probably using the `:cloud` versions (`glm-5.1:cloud`, `kimi-k2.6:cloud`) through an Ollama account. That matters because any chat app can then reach your models without your Mac being on.

## Main pick: Open WebUI

**Why it fits you**
- It's the most widely used and actively developed open-source chat app for Ollama. It connects to Ollama directly and also to any OpenAI-compatible service.
- It displays math formulas properly, which helps with homework. You can paste a photo of a problem if the model accepts images.
- It runs as a website, so on your phone you can open it and use "Add to Home Screen" to get an app-like icon. I found no reliable native phone app for Open WebUI, LibreChat or Msty.

**Install (Mac, easiest with Docker Desktop)**
```bash
# 1. Install Docker Desktop from docker.com and start it
# 2. Run Open WebUI, pointing it at Ollama on your Mac
docker run -d -p 3000:8080 \
  --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway \
  -v open-webui:/app/backend/data \
  --name open-webui --restart always \
  ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:main
```
Without Docker: `pip install open-webui` (needs Python 3.11), then `open-webui serve`, and the address is `http://localhost:8080`.

**First run**
1. Make sure Ollama is running and signed in (`ollama signin`), and pull the cloud models: `ollama pull glm-5.1:cloud`, `ollama pull kimi-k2.6:cloud`.
2. Open `http://localhost:3000`. The first account you create becomes the admin account.
3. Your Ollama models should appear in the model picker automatically. If not, go to **Admin Settings → Connections** and set the Ollama address to `http://host.docker.internal:11434`.
4. Optional: set GLM-5.1 as your default model and add a short system prompt, e.g. "Explain math step by step; use LaTeX."

**Using it on your phone and away from home**
- **Free option:** install [Tailscale](https://tailscale.com) on your Mac and phone, then open `http://<your-mac's-tailscale-name>:3000` on the phone and add it to your home screen. Your Mac has to be on.
- **Paid, always-on option:** rent a small server for about $5–10/month (for example Hetzner or DigitalOcean) and run the same Docker command there. Instead of local Ollama, connect it to Ollama Cloud with your API key under **Admin Settings → Connections**. I believe the OpenAI-compatible address is `https://ollama.com/v1`, but check Ollama's docs. Put Tailscale or a login in front of it, since it's reachable from the internet.

## If you'd rather pay than run anything yourself

- **TypingMind:** a polished hosted chat app that works on phones. You bring your own Ollama Cloud API key, and they have a [specific guide for Kimi-K2.6](https://www.typingmind.com/guide/ollama-cloud/kimi-k2.6). This is the closest to "pay a fee and it just works."
- **Ollama's own desktop app:** the simplest option and already installed. It's fine for quick questions on your Mac but has fewer features and no phone app.
- **Msty:** a nice desktop app (about $79/year for the paid tier), also with no phone app.
- **LibreChat:** good, but it's a heavier setup (four separate services). Only worth it if you need things Open WebUI lacks.

## Things to know
- **Billing:** sources conflict on how Ollama Cloud charges. Some describe Free/Pro/Max subscription tiers, while TypingMind's page lists per-token API prices. Check ollama.com/pricing before committing.
- **Newer models:** `glm-5.2:cloud` and `kimi-k2.7-code:cloud` have appeared since the versions you're using. One June report said Kimi K2.6 sometimes produces garbled text while it's reasoning, and GLM-5.1 had no such reports. Open WebUI makes it easy to try both side by side.

Sources:
- [awesome-ollama-models (cloud model list)](https://github.com/RedBeret/awesome-ollama-models)
- [Ollama Cloud vs API vs subscriptions](https://yage.ai/share/ollama-cloud-vs-api-vs-subscriptions-en-20260428.html)
- [TypingMind + Ollama Cloud Kimi-K2.6 guide](https://www.typingmind.com/guide/ollama-cloud/kimi-k2.6)
- [Open WebUI alternatives docs](https://docs.openwebui.com/alternatives.md)
- [Open WebUI vs LibreChat (docs)](https://docs.openwebui.com/alternatives/librechat.txt)
- [AnythingLLM vs Open WebUI vs LibreChat 2026 (DEV)](https://dev.to/jovan_chan_9500711396d4e6/anythingllm-vs-open-webui-vs-librechat-in-2026-which-self-hosted-ai-interface-should-you-use-24cl)
- [LM Studio vs Msty vs LibreChat vs Open WebUI (2026)](https://recapio.com/digest/lm-studio-vs-msty-vs-librechat-vs-openweb-ui-vs-anythingllm-local-ai-apps-exposed-2026-by-savage-rev)

**Recommendation: use [Serena](https://github.com/oraios/serena) as your one structured-code MCP server.** Keep ripgrep and a short AGENTS.md alongside it. Only add a semantic or vector search server if you later find a specific gap.

I'm an AI, so I can't tell you what I've "settled on" from my own use. This is my read of the tools and of how agents tend to behave with them.

## Why Serena

- **The agent actually uses it.** Its tools work at the level of symbols: find a symbol, find everything that references it, list a file's symbols, and edit or replace a whole function body. That lines up with how agents already plan work ("find X, see who calls it, change it"), so the model picks these tools up without much coaching. Vector search tools return chunks of text, which the model then has to re-read and check with grep anyway.
- **Answers come from real language servers (LSP).** Serena runs the same language servers your editor uses, for 40+ languages. "Who calls `save()`?" gets a type-aware answer instead of every line containing the string `save`. Grep struggles most with overloaded names, interfaces and similar method names across a big codebase.
- **It can edit, not just read.** It can rename and edit symbols. Codanna, CodeGraphContext and claude-context are read-only.
- **It's light to run.** You need `uv`, nothing else: no Neo4j, no Milvus, no embedding API key or cost. The language server keeps its index current as files change, so there's no separate embedding index to rebuild.
- **It has client-specific modes.** There are `claude-code` and `codex` contexts that switch off Serena tools that duplicate the client's own file and shell tools.

## What to watch for

- **Agents still fall back to grep.** Claude Code especially has strong habits around its built-in Grep and Read tools. Add one line to AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md, for example: *"For code navigation (definitions, references, call sites), prefer Serena's symbol tools over grep."* That noticeably changes behaviour.
- **Startup can be slow.** The language server can take a while to start on a big repo, and some languages need extra dependencies (see the Language Support page).
- **License change.** Serena moved to GPL-3.0-or-later around October 2026. Running it locally is fine; it only matters if you redistribute it.
- **No "find code by meaning" search.** Serena can't answer vague queries like "where do we handle retries?". For that you'd need [claude-context](https://github.com/zilliztech/claude-context), which is hybrid keyword plus vector search but needs Milvus/Zilliz and an embeddings provider. Alternatively, a graph tool like CodeGraphContext or Codanna can answer call-graph and impact questions. Several comparisons suggest the same pairing: Serena plus at most one search or graph tool.

## Is it worth it over ripgrep and AGENTS.md?

- **Probably not** for small to medium repos, especially in dynamic languages. A good AGENTS.md (layout, conventions, entry points, how to run tests) plus ripgrep gets you most of the benefit, and the extra tool descriptions also take up context.
- **Yes** for large or unfamiliar repos, statically typed languages (TypeScript, Java, Go, Rust, C#), and refactors that touch many call sites. In those cases precise lookups mean fewer wasted file reads and fewer missed call sites.
- **Cheap test:** run the same 3–5 real tasks with and without Serena and compare tokens used, wrong edits and missed references. That will tell you more than any comparison article.

## Install and first run

I'm assuming you use Claude Code or Codex on macOS. These commands come from Serena's current README and client docs. I haven't run them, so check `serena --help` if anything differs.

1. **Install uv** (if you don't have it): `curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh` or `brew install uv`
2. **Install Serena:**
   ```bash
   uv tool install -p 3.13 serena-agent
   serena init            # uses the LSP backend by default (JetBrains users: serena init -b JetBrains)
   ```
   The README says to avoid installing through MCP or plugin marketplaces because those commands are out of date.
3. **Connect it to your agent:**
   - Claude Code, quick setup: `serena setup claude-code`
   - Or manually, for all projects:
     ```bash
     claude mcp add --scope user serena -- serena start-mcp-server --context claude-code --project-from-cwd
     ```
   - Codex: `serena setup codex`, or add this to `~/.codex/config.toml`:
     ```toml
     [mcp_servers.serena]
     startup_timeout_sec = 15
     command = "serena"
     args = ["start-mcp-server", "--project-from-cwd", "--context=codex"]
     ```
   - Other clients: run `serena start-mcp-server --context ide` and add `--project-from-cwd` or `--project <path>`.
4. **First run:**
   - Start the agent from the repo root, run `/mcp`, and check that Serena is connected.
   - If it times out on a big repo, set `export MCP_TIMEOUT=60000`.
   - A local dashboard (it was on port 24282 in older versions) shows logs and language-server status.
   - Older guides pre-index with `serena project index`, which speeds up the first language-server start on large repos. Check it still exists in v2.
   - Give it a real test, e.g. *"Using Serena, find all callers of `<some function>` and summarise them."* Then check whether it used `find_referencing_symbols` or quietly went back to grep.
5. **Add the AGENTS.md nudge** from above.

# Recommended local model for Ask O11y

**My main pick is Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507, quantized to Q4_K_M, with a context window of at least 32k tokens. Plan on 24 GB of VRAM, or a Mac with 32 GB or more of unified memory.**

If you only have about 16 GB, use **gpt-oss-20b** instead. If you have 64–96 GB or more, **gpt-oss-120b** or **GLM-4.5-Air** will get closest to Haiku 4.5.

Neither the Ask O11y listing nor its GitHub README recommends any local model. They only say to configure a provider in the Grafana LLM plugin. The picks above are my own judgment. Open models change quickly, so check whether a newer version of one of these families is out before you download.

## Why Qwen 2.5 probably struggled

I'm assuming you meant Qwen2.5-14B, since Qwen 2.5 has no 13B size. Two problems likely added up:

1. **Context truncation (most likely cause).** Ask O11y sends 56+ tool definitions plus a system prompt and query results. That can easily be 10–20k tokens before your question. Ollama's default context is small (4k in many versions) and it cuts off the excess without any error. The model never sees the tools, so it fails or makes things up. Whatever model you pick, set the context length explicitly.
2. **Weak tool calling.** Qwen2.5-14B is an older model with mediocre multi-step tool use. Ask O11y is an agent: it chains queries, reads the results and calls more tools. The Qwen3-2507 and gpt-oss models are much better at this.

## Model and VRAM sizing

These are estimates: Q4 weights plus KV cache, plus about 1–2 GB of overhead.

| Tier | Model | Weights | KV cache @ 32k | Total @ 32k | Fits on |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Budget | gpt-oss-20b (MXFP4) | ~13 GB | ~1 GB | **~15–16 GB** | 16 GB GPU, or Mac with 24 GB+ |
| **Recommended** | **Qwen3-30B-A3B-Instruct-2507 Q4_K_M** | ~18.6 GB | ~3 GB (~6 GB @ 64k) | **~22–23 GB** | 24 GB GPU (3090/4090), or Mac with 32 GB+ |
| Better | gpt-oss-120b (MXFP4) | ~63 GB | ~2–3 GB | **~68 GB** | 80 GB GPU, or Mac with 96 GB+ |
| Better | GLM-4.5-Air Q4 | ~65–70 GB | ~5+ GB | **~75 GB** | 2×48 GB GPUs, or Mac with 128 GB |

How to estimate other models:
- **Weights:** at Q4_K_M, roughly 0.6 GB per billion parameters.
- **KV cache:** about 2 × layers × KV heads × head size × 2 bytes per token. For Qwen3-30B-A3B that's about 96 KB per token, so 32k tokens comes to about 3 GB. Setting the KV cache to q8 roughly halves that.
- **Dense 32B models are a poor fit for 24 GB.** Qwen3-32B, for example, needs about 20 GB for weights plus about 8 GB of KV cache at 32k, which doesn't fit. The 30B-A3B model is a mixture-of-experts model, so its cache is smaller and it runs 3–5× faster. Speed matters for an agent that makes many calls in a row.
- **On a Mac:** by default macOS lets the GPU use only about 65–75% of RAM. A 32 GB Mac gives about 21–24 GB, which is just enough for the recommended tier. Keep the context at 32k.

## Install and first run (Ollama)

I haven't run any of this on your machine. These steps are for you to run.

**1. Install Ollama and download the model**
```bash
brew install ollama          # or install the app from ollama.com
ollama pull qwen3:30b-a3b-instruct-2507-q4_K_M
# 16 GB option instead:  ollama pull gpt-oss:20b
```
Tag names change, so if a pull fails, check the tag on ollama.com/library/qwen3.

**2. Start the server with a large context (this is the key step)**
```bash
OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=32768 OLLAMA_FLASH_ATTENTION=1 OLLAMA_KV_CACHE_TYPE=q8_0 ollama serve
```
If memory allows, use 65536 instead of 32768.

**3. Check that tool calling works before involving Grafana**
```bash
curl http://localhost:11434/v1/chat/completions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{
  "model": "qwen3:30b-a3b-instruct-2507-q4_K_M",
  "messages": [{"role":"user","content":"What is the CPU usage of host web-1?"}],
  "tools": [{"type":"function","function":{"name":"query_prometheus",
    "parameters":{"type":"object","properties":{"expr":{"type":"string"}},"required":["expr"]}}}]
}'
```
The response should contain a `tool_calls` entry with a PromQL expression. Then run `ollama ps`. The model should show **100% GPU**. If part of it shows as CPU, it's spilling out of VRAM and will be slow.

**4. Point the Grafana LLM plugin at Ollama**

Go to Administration → Plugins → LLM → Configuration. Exact labels differ between versions.
- Provider: **OpenAI-compatible / Custom**
- API URL: `http://localhost:11434`. If Grafana runs in Docker, use `http://host.docker.internal:11434`. Depending on the plugin version, you may need to add `/v1` to the end.
- API key: any placeholder, such as `ollama`
- Map **both** the base and the large model to `qwen3:30b-a3b-instruct-2507-q4_K_M`. Ask O11y skills can request either class.
- Save, then use the plugin's health or test check.

**5. Tune Ask O11y**
- Set the **LLM token budget** below your context length, around 24k for a 32k context.
- Lower **max parallel tool calls** to 1–2. Local models handle sequential calls more reliably, and a single GPU handles them faster.
- If your MCP setup lets you turn off tool groups you don't need, do it. Fewer tools means a smaller prompt and better tool choices.
- Start with a simple question, such as "Which services have the highest error rate in the last hour?", before trying full root-cause investigations.

## What to expect

Even the recommended model will be noticeably weaker than Haiku 4.5. Expect more wrong PromQL or LogQL, and long investigations that stop early. The 120B-class models narrow that gap a lot. If results are still poor after fixing the context length, switch to llama.cpp's `llama-server --jinja -c 32768` or to vLLM. Both often handle tool calls more strictly than Ollama.

Sources:

# Offline phone tutor: what to build

## Main recommendation

Don't rely on one "trained" model. Build three parts:

1. **A small instruction-tuned model** (about 1–4B parameters, compressed to 4-bit so it fits on a phone) that writes the explanations.
2. **RAG over your textbooks.** RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) means the app first finds the relevant textbook passages, then hands them to the model. This is what keeps answers tied to the books and the syllabus.
3. **A tagged question bank** stored as a plain database, not inside the model. Practice works by looking up questions in that database. The model's job there is to explain and give feedback.

Do the heavy work on your computer before you ship: cleaning the textbooks, tagging questions, writing worked solutions and generating extra practice questions. A large model can help with all of that. The phone then only does lookup plus short answers. That split is the most important design decision for a tiny offline model.

**Assumptions:** mostly mid-range Android phones with 4–8 GB of RAM, English-language content, and at least one subject with maths in it. Tell me if any of these is wrong.

## Which model

| Phone RAM | Start with (well-known baselines) | Newer candidates to test |
|---|---|---|
| 4 GB | Gemma 3 1B, Qwen3 1.7B | Qwen 3.5 0.8B / 2B |
| 6–8 GB | Gemma 3 4B, Phi-4-mini (3.8B) | Gemma 4 E2B (~1.5 GB), Qwen 3.5 4B |

Check the newer 2026 models (Gemma 4 edge versions, Qwen 3.5 small) on their Hugging Face model cards. The benchmark figures I found online come from blog-style sources and contradict each other. Choose by running your own test set: about 100 real student questions plus past-paper items, scored against the mark schemes, on your cheapest target phone. Also check the licences before you ship. Qwen uses Apache-2.0; Gemma has its own terms.

For searching the textbooks you also need a small **embedding model**, which turns text into numbers so similar passages can be found. Options include EmbeddingGemma (~300M) or bge-small / MiniLM (~30–130 MB). Combine it with keyword search (BM25). Textbook terms like "mitosis" or "Le Chatelier" match very reliably by keyword. On the phone, SQLite with the sqlite-vec extension can hold both the passages and the search index.

## RAG, fine-tuning, or both?

**Use RAG for the content. Fine-tune only for behaviour, and only if you need to.**

- **Don't** try to teach a 1–4B model the textbooks by training it. Small models memorise facts unreliably and then make things up confidently. With RAG you can show the page and section each answer came from, and you can update content without retraining.
- **You can** fine-tune later with LoRA, a cheap method for adjusting a model. Unsloth on a free or cheap Colab GPU handles 1–4B models. Use it to teach *style and scope*: answer at this grade level, use the passages it was given, show working, say "that's outside your syllabus", ask a guiding question instead of handing over the answer.
- **How to make training data:**
  - Take past-paper questions and textbook-style questions.
  - Retrieve the matching passages.
  - Have a large model write the ideal tutor answer.
  - Have a teacher spot-check the answers.
  - 1,000–3,000 good examples is plenty.

  This approach is called distillation.
- **Order:** get plain RAG plus good prompts working first. Fine-tune only if your test set shows a specific problem with tone or staying in scope.

## Practice questions

1. **Find past and practice questions:** before shipping, use a big model to tag every question with subject, syllabus topic, difficulty, marks, year and its mark scheme. Have a person check the tags. On the phone, picking a topic is then a normal database query, which is instant and reliable.
2. **Mark answers:** the student answers, and the small model compares the answer with the stored mark scheme and gives feedback. Small models handle this well because the correct answer is right there in front of them.
3. **"Similar" questions:**
   - **Best option:** generate thousands of variants on your computer with a large model, have them reviewed, and ship them as part of the bank.
   - **Maths and physics:** use templates with changing numbers, and have code compute the correct answer. Never let the small model do the arithmetic.
   - **Essay and theory subjects:** letting the model rephrase questions live on the phone is acceptable, but label those questions as "generated".

## Install and first-run steps (prototype on your Mac first)

I haven't run any of these. [source], the software recommendation tool I checked, had no tested tool matching this use case, so these are standard, well-known tools.

1. **Try models on your computer.** Install Ollama from ollama.com (or `brew install ollama`), then:
   ```
   ollama pull gemma3:1b
   ollama pull qwen3:1.7b
   ollama run gemma3:1b "Explain osmosis for a 15-year-old in 4 sentences."
   ```
   For newer models, look up the exact names in the ollama.com library (Gemma 4 / Qwen 3.5 small); I'm not certain of them.
2. **Prepare the textbooks.** Convert the PDFs to Markdown with equations kept as LaTeX, using Docling or Marker. Split the text into chunks of about 300–500 tokens, each labelled with subject, chapter, syllabus code and page.
3. **Build a small RAG prototype** in Python: embed the chunks, store them in SQLite with sqlite-vec, find the top 3 chunks plus keyword matches for each question, and send them to the model through Ollama's local API. Use a system prompt along the lines of: *"Answer only from the passages. Cite the page. If the passages don't cover it, say it's outside the syllabus."*
4. **Test on a real phone.** Install Google's **AI Edge Gallery** app (Android, and iOS where available), load a candidate model, and measure speed and memory use on your cheapest target device.
5. **Build the app.** Choose one route:
   - **Google LiteRT-LM** (formerly the MediaPipe LLM Inference API): native Android/iOS, Gemma models best supported.
   - **llama.cpp**: works with any GGUF model file. Use it through `llama.rn` in React Native, or native bindings.
   - **MLC LLM**: another cross-platform option.

   As a beginner, React Native or Flutter with a llama.cpp binding plus SQLite is the gentlest path.

## Challenges and workarounds

| Challenge | Workaround |
|---|---|
| Made-up answers | Strict "use the passages" prompt, citations, a confidence check ("no matching passage → say so"), test set |
| Weak at maths and arithmetic | Show stored worked solutions; do calculations in code; let the model explain the steps, not compute them |
| Slow on phones (reading long input is costly) | 2–3 short chunks, short answers, stream the text as it's generated, cache the system prompt |
| Wide range of phone RAM | Two model sizes (1B "lite" vs 4B "full"), chosen at install time |
| Download size (model 0.5–2.5 GB + index) | Separate download per subject; sideload over USB or SD card for schools with no internet |
| Equations and diagrams in PDFs | Clean up LaTeX by hand for key chapters; show figures as images rather than asking the model to read them |
| Students drifting off-topic or misusing it | Syllabus-scope prompt, topic filter, guiding-question tutoring style, age-appropriate refusals |
| Heat and battery | Limit answer length; run the model only when needed |
| Copyright | Confirm you have the right to redistribute the textbooks and past papers inside an app |
| Updates while offline | Version your content packs so new ones can be sideloaded |

**Suggested order:** first a Mac prototype with one subject and plain RAG, then a test set, then a phone test, then the question bank, then the other subjects, and fine-tuning last and only if needed.

Sources:
- [Ertas: best models for on-device mobile AI 2026](https://www.ertas.ai/blog/best-models-on-device-mobile-ai-2026)

I'd switch to **[git-spice](https://abhinav.github.io/git-spice/)** (`gs`). It's a free, open-source CLI built for the same workflow you use Graphite for: you create stacked branches, it restacks them when a lower branch changes, it opens one PR per branch with the right base, and it updates those PRs. It doesn't need a web dashboard, an account or a paid plan. It works with GitHub and GitLab, and its commands are close enough to `gt` that you'll pick it up in an afternoon.

I'm assuming you're on GitHub with a Mac and Homebrew. I haven't checked Graphite's pricing change myself. A third-party comparison from this year still lists a free Hobby tier with the CLI, so it's worth confirming whether you really lose CLI access before you switch.

## git-spice: install and first run

**Install**
```sh
brew install git-spice
```
Ghostscript also installs a command called `gs`. If you have it, the two will clash. Check the git-spice install docs for the alternate binary name, or set up an alias.

**First run, inside a repo**
```sh
gs repo init          # pick trunk (main) and remote (origin)
gs auth login         # GitHub login: browser/device flow, a token, or reuse the gh CLI
```

**Bring over your existing Graphite stacks.** Your branches and PRs are plain git and GitHub objects, so nothing is lost. Check out each branch from the bottom of the stack up and run:
```sh
gs branch track       # (gs bt) it'll ask for or guess the base branch
```
Starting new stacks may be easier than migrating ones that are nearly done. You can finish those with `gt` while you still have it.

**Daily commands mapped to `gt`**

| What you do | Graphite | git-spice |
|---|---|---|
| New branch on top of the current one | `gt create` | `gs branch create name` (`gs bc`) |
| Commit and restack the branches above | `gt modify` | `gs commit create -m ...` (`gs cc`) / `gs commit amend` (`gs ca`) |
| Push and create/update the PRs | `gt submit --stack` | `gs stack submit` (`gs ss`); one branch: `gs bs` |
| Pull trunk and clean up merged branches | `gt sync` | `gs repo sync` (`gs rs`) |
| Rebase the stack | `gt restack` | `gs stack restack` (`gs sr`), `gs upstack restack` (`gs usr`) |
| Move around the stack | `gt up/down/top/bottom` | `gs up` / `gs down` / `gs top` / `gs bottom` |
| See the stack | `gt log short` | `gs log short` (`gs ls`), `gs ll` |

Run `gs --help` or see the docs for the full list. Command names and aliases sometimes change between releases.

## Other options

- **Aviator's `av` CLI.** Open source and also branch-per-PR, with commands like `av stack sync` and `av pr`. It's the closest match to Graphite after git-spice. It only supports GitHub.
- **git-town** (`brew install git-town`). Mature, and it works with GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket and Gitea. It handles syncing stacks very well (`git town append`, `git town sync`). PR creation (`propose`) is lighter-weight than Graphite's.
- **Commit-per-PR tools: `spr` (ejoffe/spr), `ghstack`.** You keep one branch and each commit becomes its own PR. This is a different way of working. Try it only if you like it, and note that ghstack PRs don't merge cleanly through the normal GitHub UI.
- **Jujutsu (`jj`) or Sapling (`sl`).** Version-control tools that work with git repos and make stacks feel native. jj especially makes rebasing a stack almost free. Of everything here, this would change your workflow the most.
- **GitHub's native stacked PRs.** Reportedly entered private preview in April 2026 with a waitlist. That claim comes from a vendor's comparison, so check it yourself. Keep an eye on it, but don't plan around it yet.

## If you'd rather use plain git and a few scripts

Modern git covers much of what Graphite does:

1. **`rebase.updateRefs`** (git 2.38 or newer). This handles restacking. Rebase the top branch of the stack onto `main` and git moves every branch in between with it:
   ```sh
   git config --global rebase.updateRefs true
   git config --global rerere.enabled true   # remembers how you resolved repeated conflicts
   git checkout top-of-stack && git rebase main
   ```
2. **Pushing.** Loop over the branches with `git push --force-with-lease origin <branch>`.
3. **PRs.** Use `gh pr create --base <parent-branch> --head <branch>` for each branch. After the bottom PR merges, use `gh pr edit <n> --base main` to retarget the next one.

Plain git is missing two things Graphite gives you. First, it doesn't record which branch is each branch's parent, so you'd need a naming convention or a small file to track that. Second, it won't clean up automatically after a squash-merge. You'd soon be writing those yourself, and git-spice already does both. My suggestion is to try git-spice first and fall back to scripts only if you want zero tooling.

Sources:

text:
Yes. MCP servers can run over the network using the **Streamable HTTP** transport, and the setup you describe works. The language model stays with the client. When a user asks "how many rows are in `abc`?", the client's model sends a tool call (for example, `execute_sql("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM abc")`) over HTTP to the MCP server on the remote machine. That server runs the query against the database and returns the result.

My assumptions: the database is PostgreSQL or MySQL, the remote host is Linux with Docker, and the client is Claude Code or Claude Desktop. Other MCP-capable clients work the same way.

## Main recommendation: DBHub (by Bytebase)

DBHub is an open-source database MCP server. It supports PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, SQLite and Oracle, and it runs over HTTP. It gives the model a general SQL tool, so ad-hoc questions like "count the rows in abc" work without any setup per question.

### Install and first run (on the remote server)

1. **Try it with the bundled demo database first:**
   ```bash
   docker run --rm -p 8080:8080 bytebase/dbhub --transport http --port 8080 --demo
   ```
2. **Point it at your database:**
   ```bash
   docker run -d --name dbhub -p 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 bytebase/dbhub \
     --transport http --port 8080 \
     --dsn "postgres://readonly_user:PASSWORD@db-host:5432/mydb?sslmode=require"
   ```
   - If the database runs on the Docker host itself, use `host.docker.internal` instead of `localhost` in the DSN.
   - You can also run it without Docker: `npx @bytebase/dbhub --transport http --port 8080 --dsn "..."`
3. **Secure it before exposing it.** In HTTP mode, DBHub listens on `0.0.0.0` and does **not** authenticate clients. That's why the example above binds to `127.0.0.1`. Then do one of these:
   - Put a reverse proxy (Caddy or nginx) in front with TLS plus authentication, such as a bearer token, basic auth, or OAuth.
   - Or skip public exposure and have clients connect through an SSH tunnel: `ssh -L 8080:localhost:8080 user@server`.
   - Either way, use a **read-only database user**. The model writes SQL on the fly, so the database permissions are your real safety limit. Check the current README for DBHub's own read-only option.

### Connect the client

- **Claude Code:**
  ```bash
  claude mcp add --transport http dbhub https://your-server.example.com/mcp
  ```
  With an SSH tunnel, use `http://localhost:8080/mcp` instead. The `/mcp` path is my assumption, so check it against the DBHub README.
- **Claude Desktop:** add it under Settings → Connectors → custom connector using the public HTTPS URL. Or use an `npx mcp-remote <url>` bridge in the config file.
- Then ask: *"How many rows are in the abc table?"*

## Alternative: Google's MCP Toolbox for Databases

Use this if you want more control. Instead of letting the model write any SQL, you define specific tools and their queries in a `tools.yaml` file. It also has built-in authentication, connection pooling and observability, and it supports many databases.

- Install: Docker image, Homebrew, a binary from the GitHub releases page, or `npx @toolbox-sdk/server --config tools.yaml`
- First run: write a `tools.yaml` with a `sources` entry (your database) and `tools` entries (for example, a `count_rows` SQL tool). Then run `toolbox --tools-file tools.yaml`. It serves Streamable HTTP, reportedly at `http://127.0.0.1:5000/mcp`; confirm that against the official docs.
- The docs pages show different versions, so take the current release from GitHub.

**Rule of thumb:** choose DBHub for quick, open-ended questions, and MCP Toolbox when you want to limit exactly which queries can run, for example in production or with many users.

Sources:
- [bytebase/dbhub (GitHub)](https://github.com/bytebase/dbhub)
- [@bytebase/dbhub (npm)](https://npmjs.com/package/@bytebase/dbhub)
- [googleapis/mcp-toolbox (GitHub)](https://github.com/googleapis/mcp-toolbox)
- [MCP Toolbox docs – introduction](https://googleapis.github.io/genai-toolbox/documentation/introduction)
