question: b11
text:
Yes. This is a standard MCP setup: the server runs on the remote machine using the **HTTP transport** (not stdio), and your client connects to its URL. My main pick is **DBHub** (by Bytebase). It's free and open source, works with PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB, SQL Server, Oracle and SQLite, and is built to run as a network service.

**How much is verified:** My recommendation service ([source]) had no tested tool for this case, so I haven't tested DBHub. The commands below come from DBHub's README and its install page at dbhub.ai. I'm assuming the remote machine runs Linux with Docker or Node.js 22.5+, and the database is Postgres. For other databases, only the connection string changes.

## Main pick: DBHub

**How it works:**
```
Your client (Claude Code / Desktop / etc.)  ──HTTP──▶  remote host: DBHub :8080/mcp  ──▶  database
```
The client sends "how many rows are in abc?", the model calls DBHub's `execute_sql` tool with `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM abc`, and the result comes back. DBHub also has a `search_objects` tool for looking up tables and columns. `explain_sql` and `health_check` are optional extras.

### Install and run on the remote server

**Option A: Docker**
```bash
docker run --rm --init --name dbhub \
  --publish 127.0.0.1:8080:8080 \
  bytebase/dbhub \
  --transport http --port 8080 \
  --dsn "postgres://readonly_user:password@DB_HOST:5432/dbname?sslmode=disable"
```
If the database runs on the same machine, outside Docker, use `host.docker.internal` as `DB_HOST`.

**Option B: Node (22.5 or later)**
```bash
npx @bytebase/dbhub@latest --transport http --port 8080 \
  --dsn "postgres://readonly_user:password@localhost:5432/dbname?sslmode=disable"
```

**Trying it out first:** add `--demo` instead of `--dsn` to run against a built-in sample database.

The MCP endpoint is **`http://<server>:8080/mcp`**.

### Connect from the client
- **Claude Code:**
  `claude mcp add --transport http dbhub https://your-server.example.com/mcp`
- **Clients that use a JSON config:** add `{"mcpServers": {"dbhub": {"type": "http", "url": "https://your-server.example.com/mcp"}}}`

Then ask: *"How many rows are in the abc table?"*

### Security (important)
- **Use a database user that can only read** (for example, give it only `SELECT` permission). The `execute_sql` tool runs whatever SQL the model writes.
- **Don't put port 8080 on the open internet.** DBHub has an `--auth-token` option, but its docs don't explain how it works. Instead, do one of these:
  - **SSH tunnel** (easiest): `ssh -L 8080:localhost:8080 user@server`, then point the client at `http://localhost:8080/mcp`.
  - **Reverse proxy** (Caddy or nginx) with TLS and authentication, or a private network like Tailscale or WireGuard.
- For several databases, or to set up read-only custom tools, use a `dbhub.toml` file with `--config`. Check the dbhub.ai docs for the current options.

## Alternatives (also not verified by me)
- **Google's MCP Toolbox for Databases** (`genai-toolbox`): a single Go binary that runs as an HTTP server. You write the allowed queries yourself in a `tools.yaml` file, so the model can't run arbitrary SQL. That makes it a good choice if you want tighter control.
- **Database-specific servers**, such as Postgres MCP Pro (`crystaldba/postgres-mcp`), which supports SSE and has a restricted mode. Choose one of these if you only use one type of database and want features like performance tuning.

Sources:
- https://github.com/bytebase/dbhub
- https://dbhub.ai/installation

text:
I recommend **Open WebUI**, connected to the Ollama you already have. It's the closest open-source match to the Claude website and app, and it's what most people end up using for Ollama. You get Claude-style chat, saved conversation history, LaTeX math rendering for homework, file and image uploads, and a model picker that shows every Ollama model you have, including `:cloud` ones. You can also open it on your phone and add it to your home screen, so it works much like an app.

**My assumptions:** you're on a Mac (that's what this machine is). Because GLM-5.1 and Kimi-K2.6 are far too big to run on most Macs, I'm assuming you use them through Ollama's cloud tags (for example `kimi-k2.6:cloud`).

I haven't installed or tested Open WebUI here. [source] (the tool-recommendation service I checked) also hasn't verified it. The commands below are the standard ones from its documentation.

## Install and first run (Mac)

**Option A: Docker** (the most common setup)
1. Install Docker Desktop or OrbStack, and make sure Ollama is running.
2. Run:
   ```bash
   docker run -d -p 3000:8080 \
     --add-host=host.docker.internal:host-gateway \
     -v open-webui:/app/backend/data \
     --name open-webui --restart always \
     ghcr.io/open-webui/open-webui:main
   ```
3. Open http://localhost:3000. The first account you create becomes the admin.
4. Pick `glm-5.1:cloud` or `kimi-k2.6:cloud` from the model menu at the top and start chatting. If the list is empty, go to **Admin Settings → Connections** and set the Ollama URL to `http://host.docker.internal:11434`.

**Option B: no Docker**
```bash
brew install uv
DATA_DIR=~/.open-webui uvx --python 3.11 open-webui@latest serve
```
Then open http://localhost:8080.

**For math homework:** ask something like "Solve ∫x·eˣ dx and show the steps." The answer should display as formatted equations. If you see raw `$...$` symbols instead, look for the LaTeX rendering toggle in Settings → Interface.

**To use it on your phone:** install Tailscale (free for personal use) on both your Mac and your phone. Then open `http://<your-mac's-tailscale-name>:3000` in the phone's browser and choose "Add to Home Screen." The catch is that your Mac has to be on and awake for this to work.

## Where paying makes sense

- **Ollama's cloud plan.** If you hit the free usage limits on the cloud models, Ollama sells paid tiers. That's probably the most worthwhile subscription for you, since Open WebUI itself is free.
- **Always-on hosting.** If you don't want to depend on your Mac being awake, run Open WebUI on a cheap server (about $5–10/month) or use a managed host that offers Open WebUI as a one-click app. Then point it at Ollama's cloud API with an API key instead of your local Ollama. Check Ollama's current docs for the exact API address and how it handles keys before you set this up.

## Other options

- **The models' own chat apps.** Kimi (kimi.com) and Z.ai (chat.z.ai, the makers of GLM) have free, polished web and mobile chat apps for exactly these models. You don't have to host anything. The downside is that your conversations go to those companies, so check their privacy terms first.
- **OpenRouter's chat page** lets you pay per message for many open models, including GLM and Kimi, through a hosted web chat.
- **LobeChat** is a nicer-looking alternative to Open WebUI, and it's good if you also want to use Claude or OpenAI models from the same interface.
- **Msty or Jan** are good if you only want a native Mac app and don't need phone access.
- **OvertChat** came up through [source]. It's a self-hosted alternative to Open WebUI with mobile apps and voice chat. [source] only tested that it installs on Linux; it never confirmed that chatting actually works, and it hasn't tested it on Mac. I'd treat it as something to try later, not your main setup.

text:
I've checked the plugin's docs and current local-model options. Here's my recommendation.

## Recommendation: Qwen3.6‑35B‑A3B (`qwen3.6:35b`, about 4‑bit) on Ollama, with the context window raised to at least 32K

**Plan for about 28–32 GB of VRAM.** A 32 GB GPU or a Mac with 36 GB or more of unified memory runs it fully on the GPU.

**If you only have 24 GB:** use `qwen3.6:27b`, the dense model (about 18–19 GB of weights). Or run the 35B and let Ollama push a few layers onto the CPU. Only about 3B parameters are active per token, so it stays usable.

**If you only have 16 GB:** use `gpt-oss:20b` (about 14 GB). Expect noticeably weaker multi‑step investigations than with Haiku 4.5.

**If you have 80 GB or more:** `gpt-oss:120b` or a larger Qwen3.6 tier gets closest to Haiku‑level reliability.

### Why this model, and why Qwen 2.5 probably failed
- **No official guidance:** Ask O11y's README and troubleshooting docs don't recommend any model. They only say the Grafana LLM plugin needs a configured provider. This pick is my judgement, not something the plugin authors have tested.
- **The plugin depends on tool calling:** it sends 56+ Grafana tool definitions and runs multi‑step tool loops. Small or older models break on exactly that. Qwen3.6 lists tool calling as a supported capability, has a 256K context window, and is recent enough to be much better at agent work than Qwen 2.5.
- **The likely main cause of your trouble was context size, not just the model.** Ollama's default context is only a few thousand tokens. The system prompt plus 56 tool schemas plus query results easily go past that, and Ollama cuts off the excess silently. The model then "forgets" tools or produces broken calls. The Grafana LLM plugin talks to Ollama through its OpenAI‑compatible API, which can't set the context size per request, so you have to set it on the server.
- **Assumption:** I took "Qwen 2.5 13B" to mean Qwen2.5‑14B, since there's no 13B version.

### VRAM estimate (Q4_K_M quantization)
| Model | Weights | KV cache + overhead at 32K context | Total to plan for |
|---|---|---|---|
| qwen3.6:35b (MoE, 3B active) | ~23 GB | ~3–6 GB | **~28–32 GB** |
| qwen3.6:27b (dense) | ~18–19 GB | ~3–5 GB | ~22–24 GB (tight on a 24 GB card) |
| gpt-oss:20b | ~14 GB | ~2–3 GB | ~16–18 GB |
| gpt-oss:120b | ~65 GB | ~4–6 GB | ~70–80 GB |

Weight sizes are from Ollama's listings. The KV‑cache numbers are rough, so check them on your own hardware after loading (see step 3). A 64K context adds a few more GB.

## Install and first run (for you to run; I haven't run anything)

1. **Install Ollama:** on macOS, `brew install ollama` or the app from ollama.com. On Linux, the install script from ollama.com (read it before you pipe it to a shell).
2. **Start the server with a larger context and pull the model:**
   ```bash
   OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH=32768 OLLAMA_HOST=0.0.0.0:11434 ollama serve
   # in another terminal:
   ollama pull qwen3.6:35b
   ```
   If you use the Mac app instead, run `launchctl setenv OLLAMA_CONTEXT_LENGTH 32768` and restart the app.
3. **Check it works:** `ollama run qwen3.6:35b "hello"`, then `ollama ps`. The PROCESSOR column should read `100% GPU`. If it shows a CPU/GPU split, drop to the 27b model or a smaller context.
4. **Point the Grafana LLM plugin at Ollama:** go to Administration → Plugins → Grafana LLM → Configuration.
   - Provider: OpenAI‑compatible / custom.
   - URL: `http://<ollama-host>:11434`. If Grafana runs in Docker on the same Mac, use `http://host.docker.internal:11434`. If you get 404 errors, try the URL with `/v1` added, or without it if you had added it.
   - API key: any placeholder value.
   - Model mappings: set both **Base** and **Large** to `qwen3.6:35b`.
   - Save, then use the plugin's health check.
5. **First test in Ask O11y:** ask something that needs a tool call, such as "List my data sources, then show the 5 busiest Prometheus jobs over the last hour." If the answer clearly calls tools and returns real data, the setup works. If it invents data or stops after one step, raise the context to 65536 before you change models.

**Two more tips:** Qwen3.6 "thinks" before answering, which adds delay. For faster replies, put `/no_think` in the system prompt or a skill. Plan to keep Haiku 4.5 set up as a fallback for long investigations. Even the best open model at this size will do worse than Haiku on long tool chains.

question: b09
text:
I couldn't find one open-source MCP server that does everything you listed. Below is the closest free setup, built from small open-source MCP servers, with the coding agent covering the gaps. I haven't installed or tested any of these. [source]'s tested catalogue had nothing that matched, and everything here comes from the projects' READMEs. Read each repo before you trust it with your Play credentials.

## Main recommendation: App Publisher MCP plus two helpers

| Job | Tool | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Screenshots, icon, artwork, listing text, privacy-policy draft, Play listing and image upload, `publish_android` | **[App Publisher MCP](https://github.com/seungmanchoi/app-publisher-mcp)** (MIT, npm) | Main tool |
| Tracks, promote to production, staged rollout, halt a rollout, release status | **[mcp-upload-app](https://github.com/brunosemfio/mcp-upload-app)** (Apache-2.0, macOS only) | Optional, better release control |
| Samsung Galaxy Store (and Huawei AppGallery) | **[app-store-publisher-mcp](https://github.com/qalvinahmad/app-store-publisher-mcp)** (MIT) | Optional. Glama marks it inactive and its tools are thin API wrappers |
| F-Droid | No API exists. You submit a merge request to `fdroiddata` | Agent-assisted, done by hand |

**Why App Publisher MCP comes first:** it covers the most of your list:
- It captures screenshots from a running emulator with Maestro and adds device frames and headlines.
- It generates an icon and the 512×512 Play icon.
- It generates artwork with Gemini. Upload a 1024×500 feature graphic with `playstore_upload_image`, since there's no dedicated feature-graphic tool.
- `generate_store_listing` drafts listing text and a privacy policy and gives a guide to the content rating.
- It writes metadata into the `fastlane/metadata/` folder and checks it with `validate_metadata`.
- It publishes through fastlane supply.

### Gaps and how to fill them (my assessment)

1. **Privacy policy inferred from the code, ads detection, Data safety answers.** No MCP server I found analyses the code for this. The agent (Claude Code) can do it well by reading `AndroidManifest.xml` (INTERNET permission, AD_ID permission), the Gradle dependencies (AdMob, Firebase, Crashlytics, Facebook SDK and so on) and the network calls. You then feed what it finds into `generate_store_listing`. You still have to host the policy at a public URL.
2. **Age rating.** Google has no API for the IARC questionnaire, so it's always a human step in Play Console. The best you can get is the agent pre-filling a checklist of answers so the clicking takes about two minutes.
3. **Creating a new app.** Google's API can't create an app. You create it in Play Console and upload the first build by hand. fastlane supply needs that first build before it can connect.
4. **Metadata layout.** The README lists fields like `subtitle` and `keywords`, which are iOS names. Android fastlane uses `title.txt`, `short_description.txt`, `full_description.txt`, `changelogs/<versionCode>.txt` and `images/{featureGraphic.png,phoneScreenshots/}` under `fastlane/metadata/android/<locale>/`. Check what it writes. If it's the iOS layout, have the agent convert it. This matters because **F-Droid reads that same Android fastlane layout straight from your repo**, so one copy of the metadata serves both stores.
5. **Fixing problems automatically.** Nothing does this as a feature. In practice it's the agent loop: read the supply or Play API error, fix it (version code, a text field too long, image size), then retry.
6. **Cost and privacy.** The tools are free. Image generation needs a Gemini API key, and Google offers a free tier. Your app's descriptions are sent to Google when it generates images.

## Install (macOS)

I'm assuming you use Claude Code on macOS (your system reports Darwin) with the Android SDK and an emulator already installed.

**1. Prerequisites**
```bash
brew install node fastlane
# Maestro (screenshots): its official installer pipes a script into bash. Read it first:
curl -fsSL "https://get.maestro.mobile.dev" | bash
```

**2. Google Play service account** (done in the browser)
- In Google Cloud, enable the Google Play Android Developer API and create a service account with a JSON key.
- In Play Console, go to Users & permissions, invite that account and give it release permissions.
- Store the key somewhere safe, e.g. `~/.config/google-play-console/play.json`, and run `chmod 600` on it.

**3. Add the MCP servers**
```bash
claude mcp add app-publisher -e GEMINI_API_KEY=YOUR_KEY -- npx @seungmanchoi/app-publisher-mcp

# optional: release/rollout control
claude mcp add --scope user upload-app \
  --env GOOGLE_APPLICATION_CREDENTIALS=$HOME/.config/google-play-console/play.json \
  -- uvx --from git+https://github.com/brunosemfio/mcp-upload-app.git upload-app-mcp   # needs `brew install uv`

# optional: Galaxy Store (needs Samsung commercial seller status)
git clone https://github.com/qalvinahmad/app-store-publisher-mcp.git
cd app-store-publisher-mcp && npm install && cp .env.example .env   # set SAMSUNG_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_ID / SAMSUNG_PRIVATE_KEY
claude mcp add app-store-publisher -- node "$PWD/index.js"
```

## First run

Open your app's project in Claude Code and work through these in order:

1. **Set up:** "Run `get_status`, then `configure_playstore` with my key at `~/.config/google-play-console/play.json`, then `setup_fastlane` for this Android project."
2. **Audit:** "Read the manifest, Gradle dependencies and network code. Tell me whether the app shows ads, which third-party SDKs receive user data, and give me draft answers for Data safety and the IARC questionnaire."
3. **Assets:** "Start the emulator and take store screenshots with `maestro_store_screenshot`. Generate an icon if none exists. Create a 1024×500 feature graphic. Run `generate_store_listing` using the audit results, and write everything under `fastlane/metadata/android/en-US/` in the Android fastlane layout."
4. **By hand, one time only:** create the app in Play Console, upload the first AAB, and fill in content rating, Data safety, the ads declaration and the privacy-policy URL from the drafts.
5. **Release:** "Build the release AAB, upload it to the internal track, push the listing and images, then promote to production at a 20% rollout." If anything fails, have the agent read the error, fix it and retry.
6. **F-Droid (optional):** "Draft a `metadata/<applicationId>.yml` for fdroiddata, check that the build has no proprietary dependencies, and prepare the merge request." Your app needs a FOSS licence and must build from source with no proprietary SDKs. That usually means no AdMob or Firebase, or a separate FOSS build flavour.

## Alternatives
- **[fastlane-mcp (pampas93)](https://github.com/pampas93/fastlane-mcp):** wraps Gradle and fastlane with a per-app `fastlane-mcp.yaml`. It's narrower (build and publish only), has 0 stars and no clear licence.
- **[google-play-mcp (roadhero)](https://github.com/roadhero/google-play-mcp):** calls the Play API directly with no fastlane. It's read-only for now and publishing is on its roadmap.
- **Plain fastlane** (`supply`, `screengrab`) without MCP: the most mature option, but it fills in nothing for you, as you said.

Sources:
- [App Publisher MCP](https://github.com/seungmanchoi/app-publisher-mcp)
- [mcp-upload-app](https://github.com/brunosemfio/mcp-upload-app)
- [App Store Publisher MCP (Glama)](https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/qalvinahmad/app-store-publisher-mcp)
- [fastlane-mcp (LobeHub)](https://lobehub.com/mcp/pampas93-fastlane-mcp)
- [google-play-mcp](https://github.com/roadhero/google-play-mcp)
- [vibe-coder-server: Publishing To Stores](https://github.com/siamakerlab/vibe-coder-server/wiki/Publishing-To-Stores)
- [fastlane upload_to_play_store docs](https://docs.fastlane.tools/actions/upload_to_play_store/)
- [Play Console Help: Content ratings](https://support.google.com/googleplay/android-developer/answer/9898843?hl=en)
- [Filling out App Content declarations](https://webtoapp.design/blog/configure-app-content-in-play-console)
- [Google Play Store listing requirements (PlayAudit)](https://playaudit.app/blog/google-play-listing-requirements)
- [F-Droid forum: how to publish](https://forum.f-droid.org/t/how-to-publish-my-app-on-f-droid/198)
- [How to publish an Android app on F-Droid (DEV)](https://dev.to/gargpadmakar/how-to-publish-an-android-app-on-f-droid-complete-step-by-step-guide-3j2p)
- [Best Fastlane MCP servers (Glama)](https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/integrations/fastlane)

text:
I've finished checking the main candidate's docs, so here's the answer. I ran no commands and changed no files.

## Recommendation: review **protoprimer** before you build your own

The niche isn't empty. **[protoprimer](https://github.com/uvsmtid/protoprimer)** (MIT, by uvsmtid) is very close to what you describe:

- **Single file, no setup needed:** you commit your own copy of `proto_kernel.py` next to `pyproject.toml`. It starts under whatever `python` is on `PATH`, with no venv and no packages.
- **What it does:** it restarts itself under the required Python version, downloading that version if needed. It then creates the venv, installs pinned dependencies and hands control to your code.
- **Config:** a repo-wide config plus per-environment configs, selected with `./prime --env dst/special_env`. `./prime eval` shows the merged config. The docs have pages on log verbosity, config format, env vars, the requirements lock and pip vs. uv as installer.
- **Extension points:** custom steps run after the venv exists, either through `run_boot_env_client_func(...)` or by adding nodes to its step graph (`ContextBuilder` / `StateNode`). That fits pre-commit setup, generated code and similar jobs.
- **Hand-off:** `./prime start "module:func" -- args` and app entry scripts like `./some_app` run code from the venv without activating it. `./prime shell` opens a shell with the venv active.
- **Idempotent:** you run it after every clone or pull. `./prime reset` rebuilds the venv and re-pins versions.

**How mature it is:** small and young. When I looked it had about 128 commits, 23 stars, 10 open issues, no GitHub releases, and a PyPI package. That's good if you want to contribute and shape it. It's a risk if you need stability, so pin your kernel copy to a specific commit.

The same author also has **[instant_python_bootstrap](https://github.com/uvsmtid/instant_python_bootstrap)**, described as a trivial case of protoprimer: one `bootstrap.py` next to `pyproject.toml`. That link returned 404 when I checked, so it may have been renamed or folded into protoprimer.

### Install and first run
These steps come from the README. I'm guessing where to get the kernel file, so check it against the [tutorial](https://protoprimer.readthedocs.io/latest/intro.html).

1. **Get the kernel.** Copy the protoprimer module file from the GitHub repo at a specific commit, or from the `protoprimer` PyPI package installed in a throwaway venv. Save it in your repo root as `proto_kernel.py`.
2. **Add the entry script** `./prime`, a tiny proxy that calls `proto_kernel.py`. The repo has examples (`prime`, `cmd/boot_env_example`, `cmd/start_app_example`). Make it executable.
3. **Configure** your Python version, dependencies, layout and per-environment overrides in `pyproject.toml`. Check the Config / config_format pages for the exact keys.
4. **Commit** `proto_kernel.py`, `prime` and the config, plus the lock file once one is generated.
5. **First run:**
   ```
   git clone <repo> && cd <repo>
   ./prime            # default env: get Python, create venv, install pinned deps
   ./prime eval       # check the effective config
   ./prime --env dst/special_env   # e.g. test/prod target
   ./prime reset      # rebuild venv, re-pin
   ```
6. **Updating:** the docs say changes to the source module are copied into your kernel copy when you run `./prime`.

**Things to check while reviewing:** how it gets Python (uv or python-build-standalone), whether uv is required or optional, and the lock file format. The overview pages I read didn't say.

## Other options

| Tool | Fit | Gap compared with what you want |
|---|---|---|
| **[pyprojectx](https://pypi.org/project/pyprojectx/)** (`./pw`, like `gradlew`) | Wrapper script committed to the repo, needs only Python 3.7+, config in `[tool.pyprojectx]`, `pw.lock`, aliases | Built to install and run tools and aliases, not to bring a whole dev/test/prod environment up. Doesn't install Python versions. |
| **uv** (`uv sync`, `.python-version`, PEP 723 scripts) | Handles the Python version, venv and lock very well | It's a binary you have to install first, not a script in the repo. Has no idea of per-environment layout or bootstrap hooks. Many wrappers (protoprimer included, it seems) call it from inside. |
| **zc.buildout `bootstrap.py`** | The original "commit one script, run it after clone" | Legacy, tied to buildout. Worth reading for its design history. |
| **Pants `./pants` launcher, "Scripts to Rule Them All"** | Same pattern of committing a bootstrap to the repo | Shell scripts, not Python |
| **mise, devenv/Nix, pixi** | Declarative environment setup | Need an outside tool installed first, so they aren't stand-alone |

## Bottom line
Review protoprimer first, since it matches nearly everything on your list. If its step-graph design feels too heavy, the room left is a *minimal* single-file bootstrapper (stdlib only, maybe 300–500 lines, optional uv). pyprojectx and uv each cover part of that, and protoprimer covers it with more machinery. Even then, opening an issue or PR on protoprimer is probably a better use of your time than starting a new project.

question: b05
text:
I'd split this into two steps, and Tesseract is the step to replace. First, read the scans with a modern OCR engine. Second, translate the text with a local LLM and lay it back into place. The Safari and Google results you liked come from strong OCR plus layout detection plus machine translation. You can now build the same thing locally on a Mac.

**Assumptions:** you're on an Apple Silicon Mac with at least 16 GB of RAM, the scans are mostly dark print on a light background, and they're in a European language. If the type is Fraktur/blackletter or another non-Latin script, see the notes at the end.

I haven't run any of this on your machine. [source], the tool-testing service I checked, had no tested tool for this task, so these recommendations come from the projects' own documentation and are untested.

---

## Main recommendation: Apple Vision OCR → BabelDOC + Ollama

This setup gives the result closest to Safari's: a PDF with the translated text placed over the original layout.

1. **OCRmyPDF with an Apple Vision plugin** adds a text layer to each scan. Apple Vision is the OCR engine behind Safari's and Live Text's text recognition, and it does much better than Tesseract on poor print.
2. **[BabelDOC](https://github.com/funstory-ai/BabelDOC)** is the layout-preserving engine behind PDFMathTranslate. It finds the page's text blocks, sends them to an LLM to translate, and writes the translation back into the same boxes. Its `--ocr-workaround` mode is built for scanned pages: it puts white boxes over the original text and writes the translation on top. It's meant for black text on a white background, so it handles yellowed paper reasonably but not colored backgrounds.
3. **Ollama** runs the translation model locally. BabelDOC works with any OpenAI-compatible endpoint, and Ollama provides one.

### Install
```bash
brew install uv ollama
uv tool install ocrmypdf --with ocrmypdf-appleocr   # Apple Vision plugin; check the plugin's README for exact name/flags
uv tool install --python 3.12 BabelDOC
ollama serve &                                      # or start the Ollama app
ollama pull qwen3:14b       # good multilingual translator; use qwen3:8b on 16 GB, or a ~30B model on 32 GB+
```
If the Apple Vision plugin doesn't install or work for you, plain `ocrmypdf` still runs. In that case, use the MinerU path below for OCR instead of Tesseract.

### First run (test on 5 pages first)
```bash
mkdir test && cp scans/page00{1..5}.png test/
# 1. images → one PDF with an OCR text layer (one PDF per document is also fine)
ocrmypdf --plugin ocrmypdf_appleocr --image-dpi 300 test/page001.png test/page001.pdf
# 2. translate while keeping the layout, using the local model
babeldoc --files test/page001.pdf \
  --openai --openai-base-url "http://localhost:11434/v1" \
  --openai-model "qwen3:14b" --openai-api-key "x" \
  --lang-in de --lang-out en \
  --ocr-workaround
```
Check the output PDF in the output folder. BabelDOC usually writes both a translated-only version and a bilingual version, and the bilingual one is very handy for research. If the pages look good, loop over the whole pile with a shell `for` loop and leave it running overnight. On a Mac, expect roughly tens of seconds per page, mostly spent on translation.

---

## For the hardest layouts: a vision-language document parser → Markdown → LLM translation

Some pages will be badly degraded or have complex layouts (columns, tables, marginal notes, mixed fonts). For those, it's usually more useful to get the reading order right than to reproduce the exact page look. The current leaders here are vision-language model (VLM) document parsers. They recognize text, layout, reading order and tables together, and give you each block's position on the page:

- **MinerU 2.5**, **PaddleOCR-VL-1.6** and **GLM-OCR** are at the top of the OmniDocBench benchmark (about 95–96), well ahead of the older pipelines. PaddleOCR-VL and GLM-OCR are reported to run on Apple Silicon through MLX ([comparison](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/news/25567/migliori-ocr-locali-pc-server), [PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.03264)).
- Setup for MinerU: `uv tool install "mineru[all]"`, then `mineru -p scans/ -o out/`. Run `mineru --help` to pick the VLM or MLX backend. The output is Markdown plus a JSON file with every block's coordinates.
- Then translate the Markdown block by block with the Ollama model, using a short script or any Ollama front end. For translated output in the original layout, you can paint each translated block back onto the page image at its coordinates. That reproduces what Google's camera mode does, and it's roughly 50 lines of Python with Pillow.

---

## Tips for 500–1,000 pages
- **Preprocess** the scans: deskew them, make sure they're at least 300 DPI, and convert to grayscale. `ocrmypdf --deskew --clean` handles much of this. It matters more than the choice of OCR engine.
- **Keep the source text** next to the translation, because OCR mistakes in historical print are inevitable. The bilingual PDF or a side-by-side Markdown file lets you check doubtful passages.
- **Give the LLM context** in the prompt: the period, the subject and how you want old spellings handled. This noticeably improves historical translations.
- **Fraktur or other historical scripts:** Apple Vision and the VLM parsers are weaker on these. Try Tesseract's dedicated `frk`/`deu_latf` models or Kraken for the OCR step, and keep the rest of the pipeline as it is.
- **The translation_layoutrecovery repo you tried** is an older research prototype with outdated dependencies. BabelDOC/PDFMathTranslate is the maintained successor of that idea ([ACL 2026 paper](https://aclanthology.org/2026.acl-demo.25/)).

Sources:
- [BabelDOC on GitHub](https://github.com/funstory-ai/BabelDOC)
- [BabelDOC on PyPI](https://pypi.org/project/babeldoc)
- [BabelDOC ACL 2026 demo paper](https://aclanthology.org/2026.acl-demo.25/)
- [PDFMathTranslate overview](https://blog.brightcoding.dev/2026/02/08/pdfmathtranslate-the-revolutionary-tool-preserving-scientific-layouts)
- [PaddleOCR-VL paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2510.14528)
- [PaddleOCR-VL-1.6 paper](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.03264)
- [Local OCR comparison 2026](https://pasqualepillitteri.it/news/25567/migliori-ocr-locali-pc-server)

question: b12
text:
I haven't used these in long-running daily work, so I can't tell you which one I've "settled on." What follows comes from the projects' docs, one comparison write-up, and sandbox install checks from [source]. I'm assuming you're on macOS (the environment here is Darwin), you use Claude Code or Codex, your code is mostly in typed languages, and you want something free and local.

## Main recommendation: Serena, and start without the extras

**Serena** ([oraios/serena](https://github.com/oraios/serena)) is the safest first choice:

- **How it works:** it sits on top of language servers (LSP) for more than 40 languages. That gives the agent exact find-symbol, find-references, a symbol overview per file, and edits made at the symbol level. Renames and signature changes are real refactors, not text replacements.
- **No index to build or keep fresh.** The language server does the work, so setup is mostly "install and connect." The cost is that some languages need their own language server or toolchain installed, and startup can be slow.
- **It edits code as well as reading it**, which none of the graph or vector tools do.
- **It's honest about the main problem in this space:** its own docs admit that in long sessions agents tend to drift back to grep and file reads. It ships hooks that remind the agent to use Serena and a system-prompt override to counter this. That matches your concern about whether the agent actually uses the structured data. Without some nudging, it often doesn't.

**What it doesn't do:** semantic search ("find code by meaning") or whole-repo call graphs and impact analysis. If you need those, add a graph tool next to it (see below) rather than replacing it.

### Install and first run (macOS, Claude Code)
I haven't run these. They're copied from Serena's current README and clients guide, so check them against the docs before running.

```bash
# 1. Prerequisite: uv
brew install uv

# 2. Install Serena. The docs say NOT to use an MCP or plugin marketplace; those commands are outdated
uv tool install -p 3.13 serena-agent
serena init

# 3. Connect it to Claude Code (for all projects, using the current directory)
claude mcp add --scope user serena -- serena start-mcp-server --context claude-code --project-from-cwd
#    or for one project only:
#    claude mcp add serena -- serena start-mcp-server --context claude-code --project "$(pwd)"
#    or: serena setup claude-code

# 4. If it times out on startup
export MCP_TIMEOUT=60000   # add to your shell profile
```
- For Codex, run `serena setup codex`, or add an `[mcp_servers.serena]` entry with `startup_timeout_sec = 15` and `args = ["start-mcp-server","--project-from-cwd","--context=codex"]`.
- For Cursor, use `--context ide`.

**First run:**
1. Open `claude` in your repo and run `/mcp` to confirm Serena is connected.
2. Give it a task that plays to its strengths, for example: *"Using Serena, find every caller of `X`, then rename it to `Y` and update the call sites."* Check that it calls `mcp__serena__*` tools rather than `rg`.
3. **Stop the drift back to grep (recommended):** add the Serena hooks in `~/.claude/settings.json`:
   - `SessionStart` runs `serena-hooks activate --client=claude-code`
   - `PreToolUse` runs `serena-hooks remind --client=claude-code`
   - optionally, auto-approve on `mcp__serena__*`

   Hooks are marked alpha, so get the exact JSON from the [clients guide](https://oraios.github.io/serena/02-usage/030_clients.html). You can also start Claude with `claude --system-prompt="$(serena prompts print-cc-system-prompt-override)"`.

## If you also want call graphs and impact analysis

- **codebase-memory-mcp:** a persistent local knowledge graph with tools like `trace_path` and `detect_changes` ("what does this diff touch?"). Semantic search uses an embedding model built into the binary, so no API key is needed, and it's read-only. The comparison I read suggests pairing it with Serena: the graph maps the impact and Serena makes the edits.
  - **Watch out:** the default installer also changes your agent's configuration (hooks, skills, instructions). Read the script first, or install with `--skip-config` and add the server yourself. Like any static analysis, it misses dynamic dispatch.
- **Claude Context (Zilliz):** hybrid BM25 + vector search. By default it sends code chunks to an embedding API and stores vectors in Zilliz Cloud. It's only worth it if you already run Milvus or are fine with that data leaving your machine.

**Lesser-known options from [source]**, which installs MCP servers in a sandbox and checks that they answer. They're less proven than the tools above:
- **code-cortex-mcp:** a knowledge-graph MCP server, verified on macOS arm64. Indexing and graph-augmented search worked, but the check didn't show caller lookup or call-path tracing producing results. It needs CMake and a C++23 compiler to build.
- **indexio:** lexical, semantic and hybrid search plus `who_calls`. It's local and Apache-2.0, but was verified only on Linux.
- **agent-lsp:** the same LSP-based idea as Serena, with 65 tools. It installed and answered in the sandbox, but no features were tested one by one.

If you want any of these, I can get [source]'s tested install steps.

## Is it worth it over ripgrep and AGENTS.md?

My view:
- **Start with ripgrep and a good AGENTS.md.** Current models use grep well, and a short AGENTS.md (architecture map, where things live, build and test commands) often gives more than any MCP server. It costs no context for tool definitions and has no startup cost.
- **Add Serena when you see these problems:** the agent reads whole large files to find one function, misses call sites during refactors, or the codebase is large and typed (TypeScript, Java, Go, Rust, C#). That's where exact references and symbol-level edits clearly beat text search.
- **Add a graph tool only if** you often ask "what breaks if I change this?" in code you don't know well.
- **Don't run several at once.** Every server adds tool descriptions to the context, and overlapping tools make the agent's choice of tool worse, not better.

I found no independent head-to-head benchmarks; the "fewer tokens" claims come from the vendors. The cheapest way to decide is to install Serena on your real repo, give it 3–4 refactor or navigation tasks with and without it, and compare how many tokens and wrong turns each run takes.

Sources:
- [Serena README](https://github.com/oraios/serena)
- [Serena clients guide](https://oraios.github.io/serena/02-usage/030_clients.html)
- [developertoolkit.ai: Serena, codebase-memory-mcp, Claude Context and Repomix](https://developertoolkit.ai/en/ecosystem/mcp/code-intelligence-mcp/)
- [Claude Market blog](https://claudemarket.ai/blog/best-mcp-servers-for-claude-code)
- [source] sandbox results for [indexio](https://github.com/IOServicesLabs/indexio), [code-cortex-mcp](https://github.com/tigercosmos/code-cortex-mcp) and [agent-lsp](https://github.com/blackwell-systems/agent-lsp)

text:
I didn't find one open-source MCP server that does everything on your list. My recommendation is a small stack built on fastlane-format metadata:

1. **Core: [`app-publisher-mcp`](https://github.com/seungmanchoi/app-publisher-mcp)** (MIT, npm). It comes closest to what you asked for:
   - **Icons:** generates them with Gemini and exports every Android size plus the 512×512 Play icon.
   - **Screenshots:** captures them from a running emulator using Maestro, then adds device frames and headlines.
   - **Privacy policy:** drafts one with `generate_store_listing`.
   - **Content rating:** auto-detects what the app does and gives you an Android content-rating guide.
   - **Ads and data collection:** finds them from your dependencies (for example AdMob).
   - **Metadata:** writes and validates it in the fastlane format.
   - **Publishing:** uploads to Google Play through fastlane `supply` and the Play API.
2. **Samsung Galaxy Store (and Huawei): [`app-store-publisher-mcp`](https://glama.ai/mcp/servers/qalvinahmad/app-store-publisher-mcp)** (MIT). You need a Samsung Seller Portal service account, and that requires **commercial seller status**.
3. **F-Droid: you don't need an MCP server.** F-Droid doesn't accept uploaded APKs. It builds your app from source after you open a merge request to `fdroiddata`. It reads `fastlane/metadata/android/` straight from your repo, so the same metadata covers it.
4. **Optional, for more Play API coverage: [`app-publish-mcp`](https://github.com/maksym-kyryliuk/app-publish-mcp)** (MIT, 91 tools). It includes a Data safety tool, release tracks and review management. Its docs don't mention fastlane.

**Don't use for publishing:** `roadhero/google-play-mcp` is read-only for now, and `play-console-mcp` has publishing turned off.

## What still needs you (no tool gets around these)
- **First-time Play setup:** You have to create the app in Play Console yourself, and `supply` needs at least one build uploaded manually first.
- **Play Console forms:** The content-rating (IARC) questionnaire and the ads and target-audience declarations aren't fully available through the API. The MCP can work out the answers, but you click them in once, which takes about 10 minutes. After that, updates run automatically.
- **New personal developer accounts:** Google requires a closed test with 12 testers for 14 days before production.
- **Privacy policy hosting:** It needs a public URL. GitHub Pages works and is free.
- **"Free" caveat:** Image generation uses a Gemini API key. There's a free tier, but image models may need billing turned on.
- **"Auto-fix on failure":** No server does this. The agent does it: Claude Code reads the `supply` or API error, fixes the metadata or image, and runs it again. Use `supply --validate_only` for dry runs.

## Install
Assumptions: you're on macOS with Claude Code as the MCP client, and the app is a Gradle Android project.

```bash
# Prerequisites
brew install node fastlane openjdk@17      # plus Android SDK/adb (Android Studio)
curl -Ls "https://get.maestro.mobile.dev" | bash

# Core server
claude mcp add app-publisher \
  -e GEMINI_API_KEY=YOUR_KEY -e GEMINI_MODEL=gemini-2.5-flash-image \
  -- npx @seungmanchoi/app-publisher-mcp

# Samsung/Huawei (optional)
git clone https://github.com/qalvinahmad/app-store-publisher-mcp.git
cd app-store-publisher-mcp && npm install && cp .env.example .env   # set SAMSUNG_SERVICE_ACCOUNT_ID, SAMSUNG_PRIVATE_KEY
claude mcp add app-store-publisher -- node "$PWD/index.js"
```

For Google Play:
1. In Google Cloud, create a service account and download its JSON key.
2. In Play Console, go to Users & permissions and invite that account.
3. Set `json_key_file` in `fastlane/Appfile`.

## First run
1. Create the app in Play Console. Upload a signed AAB to the internal testing track by hand once.
2. Start an emulator with the app installed, open Claude Code in the project folder, and ask:
   > "Set up fastlane for this project, generate a missing icon and feature graphic, capture store screenshots with Maestro, write the listing and a privacy policy based on the app's actual network calls, SDKs and permissions, tell me the content-rating and Data safety answers, then validate the metadata."
3. Check the privacy policy and rating answers, publish the policy on GitHub Pages, and fill in the Play Console forms once.
4. Ask the agent to "publish to the internal track," then promote the release to production when it looks right.
5. For F-Droid, commit `fastlane/metadata/android/` to your repo and open an MR to `gitlab.com/fdroid/fdroiddata`. You can check the recipe locally first with `fdroid lint` and `fdroid build`.

Note that some of these projects are young, so read each one's README before giving it your Play credentials.

text:
**Main recommendation:** Don't try to teach a tiny model the textbooks. Use a hybrid: a small instruction model on the phone, plus a local search over your content (RAG), plus a plain question bank. Do most of the hard work ahead of time on a computer with a big model, and ship the results as static data. Leave fine-tuning for later, and use it only to shape tone and format.

**My assumptions:** mid-range Android phones with 4–6 GB of RAM, English content, and at least one subject that involves math. If you need iOS, or very low-end phones, the choices below change a little, and I note where.

## 1. Which model

| Phone RAM | Model to try first | Approx. size (4-bit) |
|---|---|---|
| 3–4 GB | Qwen3 1.7B or Gemma 3 1B (Qwen3 0.6B as a fallback) | ~0.5–1.1 GB |
| 6 GB+ | Gemma 4 E2B / Gemma 3n E2B, or Qwen3 4B | ~1.5–2.5 GB |

- Test 2–3 of these on your real questions before you pick one. Rankings shift every few months, and some of the newer claims (for example about Gemma 4) come from secondary sources.
- **Licenses:** Qwen uses Apache 2.0, which is simple. Gemma has its own terms of use, so read them before you distribute the app.
- If you use Qwen3, turn off its "thinking" mode (`/no_think`). Otherwise it's slow on a phone.
- **Embedding model** (turns text into vectors for search): EmbeddingGemma-300M, or something smaller like bge-small or MiniLM. Also add plain keyword search with SQLite FTS5. Exact syllabus terms like "photosynthesis" or "quadratic formula" match very well with keywords.

## 2. Architecture: RAG plus a question bank, not a purely generative model

A 1–4B model cannot reliably memorize three textbooks. Fine-tuning facts into it produces confident wrong answers. RAG keeps answers tied to the books and within the syllabus.

**Before release, on a PC or in the cloud:**
1. **Extract** the textbooks and papers to text. Equations, tables and diagrams are the painful part, so budget time to check them by hand.
2. **Chunk** the books by section (about 200–400 words each). Tag every chunk with subject → syllabus topic → subtopic.
3. **Build a question bank.** Store each past or practice question with its marked answer, year, marks and topic tags. This needs no LLM at runtime: "practice topic X" becomes a database query. That's the most reliable feature you'll have.
4. **Use a large model to pre-generate content,** for example:
   - worked explanations for each topic and for past questions
   - common mistakes
   - "similar question" variants
5. **Have a teacher review that content,** then ship it. A big model with human review beats a tiny model working live on the phone.
6. **Bundle it all** as one SQLite file containing text, tags, embeddings (via sqlite-vec) and the FTS index.

**At runtime, on the phone:**
- **Student asks a question:**
  1. Detect the subject and topic.
  2. Run keyword and vector search, limited to that subject.
  3. Pass the top 3–5 chunks to the model with a prompt like: "Explain at high-school level using ONLY these excerpts; if not covered, say so and point to the chapter."
  4. Show the source (book, chapter, page) under the answer.
- **Practice mode:**
  1. Fetch real questions by topic first.
  2. "Generate similar" serves the pre-reviewed variants. Live generation should be clearly labeled "AI-generated, unverified."
  3. For math-like questions, use templates with random numbers, where code computes the answer. Don't let the LLM do the arithmetic.
- **Marking:** compare the student's answer with the stored mark scheme. You can let the model give hints, but the official answer must be shown alongside them.

## 3. Training (later, optional)
Once RAG works, you can fine-tune with LoRA (Unsloth on Colab is the easiest route for beginners). Train on a few thousand examples of "question + retrieved excerpts → good tutor-style answer," generated by a big model and checked by people. This improves:
- tone and format
- willingness to say "this isn't in your syllabus"

It doesn't add knowledge. Then export to GGUF (for llama.cpp) or `.task`/LiteRT (for MediaPipe).

## 4. Install and first-run steps (prototype on a laptop first)
1. **Install Ollama** from ollama.com, then:
   ```
   ollama pull qwen3:1.7b
   ollama pull gemma3:1b
   ollama pull embeddinggemma
   ollama run qwen3:1.7b "/no_think Explain osmosis for a 15-year-old in 5 sentences."
   ```
2. **Set up Python:**
   ```
   python -m venv venv && source venv/bin/activate
   pip install pymupdf sqlite-vec ollama
   ```
   Write a small script that:
   - extracts one chapter
   - chunks it and embeds the chunks
   - stores them in SQLite
   - retrieves the top chunks for a question and prompts the model
3. **Build a test set** of 50 real student-style questions per subject with expected answers. Compare the models on it.
4. **Try the model on a real phone** before writing any app code. Google AI Edge Gallery or PocketPal AI (llama.cpp-based) will do. Check speed, heat and RAM use.
5. **Build the app:**
   - Android: Flutter + `flutter_gemma` / `ai_edge_rag` (MediaPipe; the RAG part is Android-only for now).
   - Android and iOS: React Native + llama.cpp bindings (`llama.rn` / `@react-native-ai/llama`) + sqlite-vec.

## 5. Challenges and workarounds
- **Hallucination:** use retrieval only, show citations, let the model say "not in syllabus," and rely on pre-reviewed content.
- **Weak math and reasoning in small models:** use the books' worked solutions, pre-generated steps, and template questions where code computes the answer. Never trust the tiny model's arithmetic.
- **PDF extraction** (formulas, diagrams): fix it by hand, store formulas as LaTeX, and show diagram images instead of describing them.
- **App size** (1–3 GB): download the model once over Wi‑Fi on first launch. Offer a smaller model for low-end phones.
- **Speed, battery and heat:** keep prompts short (only 3–5 chunks), cap answer length, and stream the output.
- **Topic drift and misuse:** a topic classifier plus a system prompt, and refuse anything off-syllabus. Students are minors, so add basic safety filtering.
- **Copyright:** check that you have the rights to put the textbook and exam text inside an app.
- **Evaluation:** have teachers grade the outputs on your fixed test set every time you change the model, prompt or data.

Phases: (1) the question bank alone, with no LLM, which is already useful; (2) RAG explanations; (3) fine-tuning, only if the tone or format still needs work.

Sources:
- [Ertas – best models for on-device mobile AI 2026](https://www.ertas.ai/blog/best-models-on-device-mobile-ai-2026)
- [Ertas – best small LLM for local deployment](https://www.ertas.ai/best/best-small-llm-for-local-deployment)
- [PremAI – best lightweight language models](https://blog.premai.io/best-lightweight-language-models-worth-running)
- [AIMagicX – on-device AI in 2026](https://www.aimagicx.com/blog/on-device-ai-models-local-llm-guide-2026)
- [FitGap – small language models](https://us.fitgap.com/search/small-language-models-slms)
- [Margelo – Fitting RAG in your pocket (React Native)](https://margelo.com/blog/fitting-RAG-in-your-pocket)
- [ai_edge_rag (pub.dev)](https://pub.dev/packages/ai_edge_rag)
- [ai_edge_rag documentation](https://pub.dev/documentation/ai_edge_rag/latest/)
- [DEV – offline assistant on Android with Gemma 4 E2B](https://dev.to/manoj_shetty/how-i-built-a-fully-offline-ai-assistant-on-android-with-gemma-4-e2b-5a19)
- [DEV – on-device RAG for Android](https://dev.to/software_mvp-factory/on-device-rag-for-android-4a7g)
